Moving it off an automatic trigger would let a backend pull request reach human merge with **no backend suite having run on its final head**. It therefore stays automatic on `pull_request`; only draft-skipping and cancellation of superseded runs are taken. |
| Facts that removed two assumed blockers | **GHCR is not a cost problem.** Container storage and bandwidth on `ghcr.io` are *"currently free"* per GitHub's own documentation, with a commitment to at least one month's notice before that changes. The 500 MB / 1 GB Packages quotas govern npm, Maven, NuGet and Gradle — not container images. The backend image is ~500 MB, which had been read as disqualifying; it is not. #186's `docker compose pull` workflow therefore survives the move to private unchanged, except that client developers must `docker login ghcr.io` with a token carrying `read:packages`. |
| Why not self-hosted runners | They would remove the minute limit entirely — GitHub bills no minutes for them and places no plan restriction on GitHub Free organizations. **R-009's Contingency forbids it in this repository by name**: *"Do not attempt to work around either quota in-repo (no self-hosted-runner fallback, …)"*. That prohibition stands and is not reopened here. Independently, GitHub scopes the residual risk to *"anyone who can fork the repository and open a pull request (generally those with read access)"* — an empty set with one maintainer, but not empty the moment client developers are granted read access, which is a live possibility under #186. Trimming reaches the same goal with no new infrastructure and no security trade-off. |
| Sequencing | Lands as a focused pull request **after** this record is accepted, together with the Q3 hook if Q3 accepts it. |

### Q3 — Enforcement of merge governance (owner decision owed)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| The constraint | GitHub Free offers **neither** branch protection **nor** rulesets on private repositories. This is not an inference: D-013 recorded both endpoints returning `403 Upgrade to GitHub Pro or make this repository public` when `hr-platform` was last private on Free, and GitHub's current documentation gates the two features identically — *"Rulesets are available in public repositories with GitHub Free … and in public and private repositories with GitHub Pro, GitHub Team…"*. **Rulesets are not an escape hatch.** D-125 applied protection only because going public removed D-013's premise; going private restores it. |
| What is mechanically enforced on `main` today | Verified live against the API for this entry: required status check `validate` (strict); `enforce_admins=true`; `allow_force_pushes=false`; `allow_deletions=false`; `required_conversation_resolution=true`; `dismiss_stale_reviews=true`; `required_approving_review_count=0`. Two contexts are deliberately absent: `test` (D-125, path-filter deadlock) and **`independent-review`, lifted by the owner under D-142** — so that gate is already procedural rather than mechanical, and Q3 does not lose it because it is not currently held. |
| What going private on Free costs, exactly | All seven settings above cease to exist. There is no partial mode and no downgraded enforcement — the protection object is simply unavailable. |
| What the pre-push hook **can** enforce | Refusal of a direct push to `main`; refusal of a non-fast-forward (force) push to `main`; refusal of a branch deletion; and running the full `validate` equivalent locally before any push succeeds. Drafted and tested against this worktree; `shellcheck` clean. |
| What the pre-push hook **cannot** enforce, and this is the crux | **It never runs on the path that actually merges.** Pull requests are merged on github.com, through the UI or API; that operation does not pass through any local hook. So conversation resolution at merge, a required green check at merge, `enforce_admins`, and protection against a force-push or branch deletion performed through the web interface or API all lose their enforcement entirely and gain **no** substitute. The hook covers the *push* boundary; branch protection covered the *merge* boundary. They are not the same boundary, and describing the hook as a replacement for branch protection would be false. |
| Second limitation, stated plainly | The hook is client-side and `--no-verify` bypasses it. With one maintainer this is tolerable — it prevents accidents and binds automated agents, which is most of its value — but it is not a control that survives an actor who does not want to be bound, and it is weaker than `enforce_admins`, which bound the owner too. |
| Option A — accept the loss (**rejected**, recorded for completeness) | Go private on Free. Merge governance becomes **entirely procedural**: no required check, no conversation-resolution gate, no admin enforcement — the exact condition R-008's own history says procedure alone failed to hold, PR #126 having lost a ten-second race to it. Cost: $0. **The state transition this would require, stated precisely because "reopen R-008" is not one:** R-008's Status is *already* `Open — Accepted Residual Risk`, so there is nothing to reopen. What would actually be required is **replacing its Mitigation**, which currently opens *"Mechanically enforced as of 2026-08-29 (D-125)"* — a sentence that becomes false the moment protection disappears — with the procedural-only state, and recording a **fourth realisation** if a merge then bypasses the process. Leaving that Mitigation standing while the mechanism is gone would be the worst outcome available: a register asserting enforcement that no longer exists. |
| Option B — buy enforcement first | GitHub **Team** at $4/user/month restores branch protection and rulesets on private repositories and raises included minutes from 2,000 to 3,000. At one seat this is **$4/month**, and with Q2's trimming nothing exceeds the allowance, so $4/month is the whole cost. R-008's mitigation survives intact. |
| **Decision: Option B** (owner, 2026-09-09) | GitHub-enforced merge governance is preserved. **Option A is rejected as the permanent private-repository model** — the repository will not be flipped private with branch protection knowingly downgraded to procedure-only enforcement. |
| Consequence while Team is unfunded | The repository **stays public**. This is the one outcome that keeps every enforcement setting intact at zero cost, and it costs only the confidentiality that Q1 wants — deferred, not abandoned. **R-008's mitigation therefore survives unchanged** and is not reopened. |
| What unblocks Q1 | Funding one GitHub Team seat ($4/month). At that point visibility flips and every setting in the row above is re-applied and verified with `scripts/check-branch-protection.sh` before the change is called done. |
| Explicitly not authorised | Flipping visibility private on the Free plan, in any circumstance, without Team in place. If that is ever proposed again it is a **new** decision superseding this one, not an implementation detail of it. |

## D-224: Degraded-Review Procedure For A Reviewer-Service Outage

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **Accepted 2026-09-09 by the repository owner**, subject to the bootstrap condition below. Acceptance changes who may satisfy D-121's gate, which R-009 requires be *"a separately approved policy change that updates the canonical workflow first"* — so `AGENTS.md` and R-009 are amended in the same branch as this entry. |
| **Bootstrap condition — this procedure may not authorise its own adoption** | **D-224 does not apply to the pull request that introduces it.** #188 must receive a **normal independent review from `chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]` on its exact final head** before this entry becomes canonical policy. A degraded-review procedure that admits itself under its own terms would have no independent check on the one change that weakens the gate — the failure mode this entry exists to prevent. Until #188 merges after a normal round, D-224 is accepted-but-not-in-force and **no pull request may rely on it**. |
| When the 14-day clock starts | At **#188's merge**, not at acceptance — a procedure that is not yet in force cannot expire. Recorded explicitly because "14 days from acceptance" would otherwise burn the window while waiting for the bootstrap review. |
| Owner | Repository owner |
| Why this exists | D-222 closed with a condition on itself: *"If a third arises for the same reason, the answer is to fix the review pipeline (R-009's territory) or to define a documented timeout with a named substitute reviewer, not to keep spending the override."* Two overrides were taken on 2026-09-09 because the reviewer produced nothing. Three pull requests (#182, #186, #187) are now in the same state. This entry is that condition being discharged rather than a third override being spent. |
| What this is **not** | **It is not D-222 and must never be used as one.** D-222 is for a merge whose *delay is itself a harm* — a defect live in production, a security exposure, a data-integrity fault still running. Reviewer unavailability is **not** a qualifying reason under D-222 and this entry does not make it one. D-222 overrides the gate for a specific merge; D-224 **degrades** the gate for a stated outage window and demands a substitute in the gate's place. A pull request merged under D-224 was not merged past the gate — it was merged under a weaker gate, and it must say so. |
| Correction that shaped this entry | The three pull requests were repeatedly described in working discussion as having received *no response* from the reviewer across six requests. **That was wrong, and the error was mine: I counted review objects and comment totals without reading the comment bodies.** The connector answered every request. Between 10:30:36Z and 11:17:11Z on 2026-09-09 it posted **seven** comments across the three pull requests, each the literal *"You have reached your Codex usage limits for code reviews."* This is not an unexplained outage. It is **R-009 realised again**, matching that risk's stated trigger word for word. |

### Criterion 1 — declaring the reviewer unavailable

| Path | Condition | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) Self-declared exhaustion, still current** | A usage-limit comment exists **and is the reviewer's most recent artefact of any kind anywhere in the repository, in any pull-request state** — nothing has landed after it, on this pull request or any other, open, closed **or merged**. The merged case is the one that bites: the pull request proving recovery is usually the one that just merged. The check **fails closed** — a fetch or parse error exits 3 rather than reporting an empty artefact set as "no recovery". A historical usage-limit comment proves the outage *happened*, never that it *persists*: quota recovers on its own, and on 2026-09-09 it recovered roughly 80 minutes after the last such comment. **The moment any round lands anywhere, path (a) is closed** — see Criterion 5. | Line 2 of the command below reading `PASS`. |
| **(b) Silence** | All of: `@codex review` requested at least **twice**, the requests at least **60 minutes** apart, the first at least **4 hours** ago; **and** no round on the current head — counting **both** review objects **and** D-158 clean-round comments, because a round that finds nothing posts a comment and no review object at all, so counting reviews alone reports "silence" on a head that was reviewed clean. | Lines 1 and 3 of the command below reading `PASS`. |

Neither path may be declared by inference, impatience, or a summary. **Every line the command prints must read `PASS` for the path being claimed; a `FAIL` or `n/a` on any required line means the gate is not degraded and the merge waits.** The command proves each prerequisite rather than reporting two counts a reader must interpret — an earlier draft returned only `reviews_on_head` and a repository-wide quota-comment count, either of which could read `0`/`n` for an unrequested, too-recent, already-reviewed, or already-recovered head.

```bash
set -o pipefail
PR=<number>; BOT=chatgpt-codex-connector; REPO=workin-hr/hr-platform
die() { echo "FAIL  evidence incomplete: $1 -- refusing to certify exhaustion" >&2; exit 3; }

# Resolve the target head FIRST and abort if it cannot be resolved. An empty
# SHA must never reach the round-count logic: `[ "" -eq 0 ]` is a bash error,
# the `if` falls through to its else branch, and the check prints a confident
# verdict about a gate it never examined -- with exit 0.
SHA=$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json headRefOid --jq .headRefOid) || die "cannot resolve #$PR"
case "$SHA" in
  [0-9a-f][0-9a-f][0-9a-f][0-9a-f][0-9a-f][0-9a-f][0-9a-f][0-9a-f]*) : ;;
  *) die "head of #$PR is not a sha ('$SHA')" ;;
esac
[ ${#SHA} -eq 40 ] || die "head of #$PR is not a full sha ('$SHA')"
SHORT=${SHA:0:7}
J=$(gh pr view "$PR" --repo "$REPO" --json reviews,comments) || die "cannot read #$PR"
now=$(date -u +%s); ep(){ date -u -d "$1" +%s 2>/dev/null || echo 0; }

# 1. no round on THIS head -- review objects AND D-158 clean-round comments
rounds=$(jq -r --arg b "$BOT" --arg s "$SHA" --arg p "$SHORT" '
  [(.reviews[]|select(.author.login==$b and .commit.oid==$s)),
   (.comments[]|select(.author.login==$b and (.body|test("Reviewed commit.{0,4}"+$p))))]|length' <<<"$J")
[ "$rounds" -eq 0 ] && echo "PASS  no round on head $SHORT" \
                    || echo "FAIL  $rounds round(s) on head $SHORT -- the gate is SATISFIED, not degraded"

# 2. path (a): the reviewer's latest artefact ACROSS THE REPOSITORY, in any
#    pull-request state. Two repo-wide endpoints, newest-first -- not a loop
#    over open pull requests: the PR that proves recovery is usually the one
#    that just merged, and `--state open` cannot see it. Fails CLOSED, because
#    an evidence check that degrades to "no artefacts found" on a transient
#    error would certify exhaustion it never established.
BOT_RE='^chatgpt-codex-connector(\[bot\])?$'   # REST says "[bot]"; GraphQL does not

# --paginate, not a single page. The two feeds are capped INDEPENDENTLY, and
# they churn at different rates -- this repository carries ~726 review comments
# to ~212 issue comments. A recovery posted as a review comment can therefore
# fall off page one of the fast feed while a stale usage-limit notice survives
# on page one of the slow one, and the merge then reports exhaustion that ended
# hours ago. Page one holds the newest 100 comments from EVERYONE, not the
# newest 100 from the reviewer.
issue=$(gh api --paginate "/repos/$REPO/issues/comments?sort=created&direction=desc&per_page=100") || die "issue comments"
prc=$(gh api --paginate "/repos/$REPO/pulls/comments?sort=created&direction=desc&per_page=100")   || die "review comments"

# --paginate emits one array per page, so flatten with .[][] rather than .[].
latest=$(jq -s --arg re "$BOT_RE" '
   [ (.[0][][] | select(.user.login|test($re)) | {at:.created_at,
        kind:(if (.body|test("usage limits";"i")) then "quota" else "round" end)}),
     (.[1][][] | select(.user.login|test($re)) | {at:.created_at, kind:"round"}) ]
   | sort_by(.at) | last // empty' <(jq -s . <<<"$issue") <(jq -s . <<<"$prc")) || die "parse"

if [ -z "$latest" ]; then echo "n/a   reviewer has posted nothing in this repository"
elif [ "$(jq -r .kind <<<"$latest")" = "quota" ]; then
  echo "PASS  exhaustion is current repository-wide ($(jq -r .at <<<"$latest"))"
else
  echo "FAIL  reviewer RECOVERED at $(jq -r .at <<<"$latest") -- D-224 has lapsed, use the normal gate"
fi

# 3. path (b): two requests >=60min apart, first >=4h ago
reqs=$(jq -r '[.comments[]|select(.body|test("@codex review"))|.createdAt]|sort|.[]' <<<"$J")
n=$(grep -c . <<<"$reqs")
if [ "$n" -ge 2 ]; then f=$(ep "$(head -1 <<<"$reqs")"); l=$(ep "$(tail -1 <<<"$reqs")")
  [ $(( l - f )) -ge 3600 ] && [ $(( now - f )) -ge 14400 ] \
    && echo "PASS  path (b): $n requests, $(( (l-f)/60 ))min apart, first $(( (now-f)/3600 ))h ago" \
    || echo "FAIL  path (b): needs >=2 requests >=60min apart and >=4h elapsed"
else echo "n/a   path (b) not claimable -- $n request(s)"; fi
```

A round on an earlier head is evidence about that head and no other.

### Criterion 2 — the remedy is attempted before the substitute

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Mandatory first step | Under path (a) the cause is known and the remedy is documented: R-009 states the mitigation is *"restoring or funding the named reviewer, not monitoring."* **The owner must either restore the quota or explicitly decline to, and the declining is recorded.** Building a substitute reviewer while an unattempted paid fix exists is precisely the *"reviewer-availability problem being paid for with governance"* that D-222 named and refused to normalise. |
| Why this clause is load-bearing | Without it, D-224 becomes a standing alternative to funding the reviewer, and the gate quietly degrades permanently. The substitute is for the window between the outage and the remedy — not instead of the remedy. |

### Criterion 3 — the replacement independent verification

All five are required. Any one missing means the gate is not degraded but simply unmet, and the merge waits.

| # | Requirement |
|---|---|
| 1 | **A read-only review pass on the frozen final head** by a reviewer with **no authorship, implementation, generation, or repository-write involvement in the change under review, on any branch** — not merely one that personally ran no `git commit`. An agent that wrote or generated the diff is an implementer under `AGENTS.md` whoever committed it, and a later read-only pass by that same agent does not launder it into a reviewer. The head must not move during or after the pass. |
| 2 | **Findings posted to the pull request verbatim**, not summarised, including findings the implementer disputes — with the dispute stated as a reply rather than by omission. |
| 3 | **Red-before-green evidence for every behavioural change**: the test failing without the fix and passing with it, run standalone, linked. |
| 4 | **The full suite green on the final head**, linked by run or local summary. |
| 5 | **A written statement of what the substitute did not cover** relative to a real round — at minimum that it is a different reviewer of unmeasured comparability, and that no independent party verified the implementer's dispositions. |

### Criterion 4 — the record required on each pull request

Posted as a single comment before the merge, containing: the head SHA; which unavailability path was declared, with its evidence; the quota-restoration decision and who made it; the substitute reviewer's identity and confirmation it holds no write access to the branch; every finding and its disposition; what remains unverified; and a link to this entry. A merge under D-224 without this comment is a policy breach, on the same terms D-222 sets for its own record.

### Criterion 5 — returning to the normal gate

| Trigger | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Any evidence that quota has recovered** — a round on any head, or any reviewer artefact that is not a usage-limit notice | The degraded procedure **lapses immediately** and the normal D-121 gate resumes for every open pull request, including those mid-flight. Recovery is the trigger, **not** the arrival of a round on the specific pull request in hand: waiting for a per-PR round would leave a window in which a stale usage-limit comment still authorised the substitute after the outage had ended. Line 2 of Criterion 1's command is what closes that window. |
| **14 days** from acceptance | Lapses automatically. Extension requires a new owner decision, not a renewal by silence — this is the clause that stops a temporary procedure becoming the standing one. |
| Either way | Every pull request merged under D-224 is listed in the extension or closure record, and each gets a retrospective round or an explicit, recorded owner decision not to seek one. |

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Amendments required on acceptance | D-224 changes which agent may satisfy the independent-review gate, so the amendment set is everything that encodes the current answer, not only the policy file: (1) **`AGENTS.md`** Mandatory Workflow — the *"unavailable, not waived"* sentence gains D-224 as its documented, time-boxed exception; (2) **R-009** — its *"not substitutable"* clause gains the same reference, which that clause explicitly anticipates; (3) **`docs/agents/responsibility-matrix.md`** — its reviewer note ends *"the gate is unavailable, not waived"* and must carry the exception; (4) **`docs/bootstrap/manual-setup-checklist.md`** step 5 — it states *"no other reviewer substitutes for it"*, which contradicts an accepted D-224 as written. All four are amended in the same branch as this entry. |
| Reviewed and found not to need amendment, with the reason | **`scripts/validate_phase0.py`'s `validate_independent_reviewer_declaration()` and its regression tests in `scripts/test_validate_phase0.py`.** The property they enforce is that `AGENTS.md` names the independent reviewer inside the workflow it gates and that `docs/agents/responsibility-matrix.md` carries a matching read-only row. **D-224 does not change that property**: `chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]` remains *the* named reviewer, and the substitute is a degraded fallback for its unavailability, not a second reviewer of record. Widening the validator to accept a substitute name would weaken exactly the binding D-121 relies on. Verified green against this branch. |
| Application to #182, #186 and #187 | **None by this entry.** D-224 defines a procedure; it merges nothing and authorises nothing retroactively. Whether to apply it to the three open pull requests, restore the Codex quota, or continue waiting is the owner's decision, taken after this record is accepted. |
| Related | **D-121** (the gate), **D-222** (the override, deliberately distinct), **D-142** (what happened last time the gate was worked around at scale — twelve pull requests merged without a round), **R-008**, **R-009**, `AGENTS.md` Mandatory Workflow. |

## D-225: Should `independent-review` Be A Required Status Context Again?

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **Accepted 2026-09-09 by the repository owner — Option A.** `independent-review` is restored as a mechanically required status context on `main`, subject to the sequencing condition below. Raised by R-008's fourth realisation and deliberately kept out of that incident's remediation (#190, #191): this is a standing governance change, and deciding it inside an incident fix is how a change of this weight avoids scrutiny. |
| **The decision is recorded now; the setting is not changed now** | This entry is the decision. The branch-protection change is a separate, later act, gated on the sequence below — recording an intent and applying a setting are different things, and conflating them is how a condition gets skipped once the record says "Accepted". |
| Required sequence, in order | **1.** #189 merges, correcting D-224's eligibility checker. **2.** D-224 is verified in force and usable — its command run against a real pull request and producing the right verdict, not merely present in the log. **3.** `independent-review` is added to `main`'s required status contexts. **4.** The **actual** protection state is verified with `scripts/check-branch-protection.sh`, not assumed from the API call that set it. |
| Why the condition is not a formality | Requiring the context while D-224 cannot be relied on recreates exactly D-142's deadlock — every pull request unmergeable during a reviewer outage — but backed by a documented procedure that does not yet work. That is worse than the current state, because the procedure's existence would be cited as the reason the deadlock is acceptable. |
| Owner | Repository owner |
| The question | `independent-review` is **not** a required status context on `main`. `validate` is the only one. Should the review gate be mechanically required again, or stay advisory? |
| How it came to be advisory | **D-142.** The Codex quota was exhausted mid-review and stayed out; with `independent-review` required, every pull request was unmergeable through no fault of its author. The owner lifted the context and twelve pull requests merged without an independent round. That was a reasonable response to a real deadlock — the objection it answered is not hypothetical. |
| What that costs, now measured rather than predicted | A commit carrying a green `validate` is admissible to `main` **whether or not anyone reviewed it**. On 2026-09-09 an agent pushed a branch to `main` directly; protection was fully applied — `enforce_admins=true`, force-pushes and deletions forbidden — and did not stop it, because the gate that would have is not required. R-008 had realised three times before as a *procedural* failure; this is the first time it realised with protection correctly configured, which is what makes it evidence about the configuration rather than about discipline. |
| What has changed since D-142, and why the question is worth reopening now | D-142's premise was that an outage leaves no path forward, so the gate must be liftable. **D-224 now supplies that path** — a time-boxed degraded-review procedure with objective unavailability criteria, a mandatory attempt at the documented remedy first, a substitute verification, a per-pull-request evidence block, and automatic lapse on recovery or after fourteen days. The deadlock D-142 responded to now has a defined, recorded route through it that does not require dismantling the gate. |
| Option A — restore it as required | The gate becomes mechanical again. A reviewer outage no longer deadlocks the repository, because D-224 is the documented route through one. Cost: every merge depends on a third-party service being reachable, and D-224's procedure is heavier than merging. |
| Option B — leave it advisory | No change. Merge governance stays procedural and depends on the tooling and the people being careful — which is precisely what failed on 2026-09-09, and what R-008's own history says procedure could not hold (PR #126 lost a ten-second race to it). Cost: $0 and no new friction; the risk is that the next tooling defect has the same reach as this one. |
| Recommendation, with its condition | **Option A, but not yet.** Requiring the context is only safe once the outage route is genuinely usable, and D-224 is currently *accepted but not in force*: its eligibility checker is still being corrected under #189, and until that merges the check can authorise a substitute the policy forbids. Restoring the requirement before then would recreate D-142's deadlock with a procedure that cannot yet be relied on. **Sequence: land #189, confirm D-224 is in force, then restore the context and verify with `scripts/check-branch-protection.sh`.** |
| Not in scope | Whether `test` should also be required. D-125 dropped it deliberately — `Backend Validate` is path-filtered and would deadlock docs-only pull requests — and that reasoning is untouched by this. A separate question if anyone wants to raise it. |
| Related | **R-008** (fourth realisation), **D-142** (why it was lifted), **D-121** (the gate), **D-224** (the outage route), **D-125** (the protection applied), **D-223 Q3** (the decision to preserve GitHub-enforced governance, whose value this incident tests). |

## D-226: The Independent Reviewer Is A Read-Only Review Agent, Not Codex

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **Accepted 2026-09-09 by the repository owner**, on the third explicit instruction to stop depending on Codex and review through a skill instead. |
| Owner | Repository owner |
| Supersedes | **D-121**'s reservation of the independent-review gate to `chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]`. D-121's *substance* — that the gate exists, covers the whole pull request, must land on the final head, and is discharged by someone who did not write the change — is untouched and restated below. Only the named party changes. |
| Decision | The independent review required by `AGENTS.md`'s Mandatory Workflow is performed by a **read-only review agent** invoked through a new `independent-review` skill. It **supersedes** the unmerged `degraded-independent-review` skill written for D-224 on branch `feat/degraded-review-skill`; that branch must be dropped rather than merged, or the repository would carry two skills for one gate. Nothing is renamed on `main`, where neither existed. `chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]` remains welcome and its rounds still count, but it is no longer the *only* party who can satisfy the gate. |
| Why now, stated honestly | Not because the reviewer misbehaved. Because it was **unavailable for most of 2026-09-09** — R-009 realised three times in one day, with recovery windows of minutes — and the repository had accumulated an unmergeable stack behind a gate nothing could satisfy. A gate that cannot be satisfied is not a control; it is an outage with a governance label on it. |
| What the reviewer must be | A pass with **no authorship, implementation, generation, or repository-write involvement** in the change under review, on any branch. An agent that wrote the diff cannot review it by later running read-only — that is the same actor twice, and `AGENTS.md`'s rule that writing automation is an implementer and never a reviewer is what forbids it. |
| The weakness, recorded rather than glossed | A read-only agent dispatched by the implementing session is **weaker** than an independent service. It shares a model family with the implementer and is invoked by it, so it is not independent in the way a third party is. What it does provide is a reviewer that did not write the code, **is instructed not to write to the repository**, and reports findings the implementer must post verbatim. **Not "cannot": that claim was in an earlier draft and was false.** Read-only agent definitions in this repository grant `Bash`, which they need to run `git diff` and `gh api` at all, and the permission deny-list does not cover plain `git push`, `gh pr merge`, `gh pr review` or `gh api -X POST`. Making it true needs a dedicated agent definition whose tool set excludes Bash-mediated writes; a repository-wide deny-list is the wrong instrument, because it would equally block the implementer, who legitimately pushes. Until that definition exists, the reviewer's read-only status is a **configuration intention, not a proven property**, and this record says so rather than implying otherwise. That is a real check and a real reduction in independence at the same time, and both halves belong in the record. |
| Evidence that it is not theatre | Its first use, on **#190**, found that the incident record this repository had just written was **factually wrong**: it claimed the merged head received zero reviewer rounds, when `ec016e4e` was reviewed at 14:03:20Z — 17 seconds after the push — with three findings that remain open on `main`. Codex's own round had produced those findings; nothing in the repository had noticed them. The substitute reviewer read the API and caught it. |
| What does not change | The gate still covers the whole pull request. It still must land on the **exact final head**. Findings are still fixed, or answered on the thread with a reason, before merge. A green CI run still proves automated verification only. **Implementers still cannot merge their own work.** D-222's override and its conditions are unaffected. |
| What this makes of D-224 | D-224 was the *temporary* degraded procedure for a reviewer-service outage. With the gate no longer depending on a single external service, its purpose narrows sharply: it remains the recorded procedure for the case where **no** qualifying reviewer can be obtained at all, and its evidence and lapse rules stand. It is no longer the expected path. |
| What this makes of R-009 | The Codex half of that risk stops being able to block merging outright. The risk stays open for the GitHub Actions half, and because losing the named reviewer is still a real degradation of independence — now recorded as an accepted trade rather than an outage. |
| Amendments this requires, per R-009's own rule | Policy **and the code that enforces it**, because prose alone would leave the rule true and its enforcement silently absent: `AGENTS.md` Mandatory Workflow **and its Global Rules bullet**; **R-009**; `docs/agents/responsibility-matrix.md` **including a row for the new reviewer**; `docs/bootstrap/manual-setup-checklist.md` step 5; `docs/bootstrap/open-questions.md`; `.github/workflows/independent-review-gate.yml`; `scripts/validate_phase0.py`; `scripts/check-review-dispositions.sh`; and their regression tests. All in this branch. |
| What the enforcement change does and does not buy | The gate now recognises an agent round through a **SHA-bound marker**, so a round cannot be recycled onto a head the reviewer never saw. The marker is body text, so it is **forgeable — but only by someone who can already write to this repository**. The gate counts a round only from an `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or `COLLABORATOR` (**amended by D-228**: repository permission `admin`/`write`, read from the collaborators API, because association depends on organisation membership visibility and reported a repository admin as `CONTRIBUTOR` to the workflow's own token), and only from a comment that has not been edited since it was posted; `CONTRIBUTOR` is excluded because one merged commit earns it and it grants no write access. Without those predicates the marker was postable by any GitHub account at all, which on a public repository meant a stranger could green the gate on somebody else's pull request. What remains is **self-attestation by the implementer**: it proves a writer claimed a round *naming this head*; it does not prove a review happened. Unlike a Codex round's `user.login`, it is not evidence of who reviewed. The compensating control is `check-review-dispositions.sh`, which refuses when a round is claimed but no finding thread and no explicit zero-findings declaration exists — and which applies the same author, edit and anchoring rules, so it cannot be armed or disarmed by anyone the gate would not count. Silence stops being a pass. |
| Rollback | Revert the adopting merge commit. The four documents return to D-121, and the workflow, validator and disposition script return to Codex-only attribution. No data migration, no state to unwind. |
| **Bootstrap — D-226 does not authorize its own adoption** | **D-226 may not review or admit the pull request that introduces it.** *The adopting pull request* — whichever one lands this entry on `main` — must be reviewed and admitted under the policy canonical **immediately before** D-226: with `chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]` as the named reviewer, or through **D-224**, that policy's own documented answer to the reviewer being unobtainable. D-226 commences at **the merge commit that lands it on `main`**, and only from that commit may a review agent satisfy the gate. **No condition here is keyed to a pull-request number**: the first draft was, the numbered pull request was then closed and reopened, and the commencement condition became unsatisfiable while reading like a typo. |
| **No retroactive effect** | D-226 says nothing about pull requests merged before it became canonical, and confers no authority over them. A review performed before D-226's adopting merge is not a D-226 review and must not be recorded as one — including reviews of #190, #191 and #192, which are prerequisites of nothing here and must be admitted on their own terms. |
| Why this clause exists | Without it the decision is circular: the rule being introduced would authorize the mechanism used to merge the pull requests it was stacked behind. That is the same shape as an override citing itself as precedent, and it is why #193 was detached from the remediation stack and rebuilt directly on `main` — so it can merge **first**, on the old policy's authority, rather than last on its own. |
| What the skill cannot enforce | Three gaps, recorded because the skill reads as though it closes them. The implementer **chooses the diff** handed to the reviewer, so a partial or wrong-commit diff still ticks every checklist item -- mitigated by requiring the reviewer to fetch the diff itself from the API and echo the SHA and file count it actually read. Independence is **self-attested** by the party whose independence is in question. And "post findings verbatim" is **unverifiable** unless the reviewer's raw output is preserved -- so the evidence comment must carry that output as a fenced block, separate from the implementer's dispositions, where omission becomes visible. |
| Related | **D-121** (superseded in part), **D-222** (override, unaffected), **D-224** (the bootstrap route, and afterwards narrowed to "no qualifying reviewer obtainable at all"), **D-225** (whether the context becomes required again), **R-008**, **R-009**. |

## D-228: The Round Recorder Is Authorised By Repository Permission, Not `author_association`

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **Accepted 2026-09-11 by the repository owner**, on being shown that the D-226 agent-round mechanism had never once been counted and could not be. |
| Owner | Repository owner |
| Amends | **D-226**'s enforcement clause, "The gate counts a round only from an `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or `COLLABORATOR`". D-226's substance is untouched: the reviewer is still a read-only agent, the round still binds to the exact head, the comment must still be unedited, and implementers still cannot merge their own work. Only the authorisation *mechanism* changes. |
| Decision | `independent-review-gate.yml` authorises the account recording an agent round by its **repository permission**, read from `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators/{login}/permission`, and accepts only `admin` or `write` (`ROUND_AUTHOR_PERMISSIONS`). The `author_association` filter is removed, and `validate_phase0.py` now **fails** if it reappears. `scripts/check-review-dispositions.sh` uses the same authority, so the compensating guard and the gate answer the same question. |
| The defect, measured | `author_association` is derived from **organisation membership visibility** as well as access. The repository owner's own round comment on #195 reported `MEMBER` to their personal token and **`CONTRIBUTOR`** to an unauthenticated caller -- which is what `GITHUB_TOKEN` is for a private membership. The gate therefore logged `#195: 0 round(s) on this head (codex: 0, agent: 0)` for a head that eleven independent review rounds had been run against (as agent reviews, not as GitHub review objects -- #195 carries none of those), with the marker present, the SHA matching exactly and the comment unedited. Measured, and stated exactly: this repository has **171** pull requests, and **exactly one** agent-round comment has ever been posted on any of them -- the one on #195 described above. It was not counted. So the mechanism has never produced a counted round, not because rounds were rejected in bulk, but because the only one ever recorded could not be. |
| Why not the two cheaper fixes | Making the membership public would fix it by publishing a fact about a person's identity to satisfy a CI check -- the wrong thing to trade. Adding `CONTRIBUTOR` to the allowlist would fix it by letting anyone who has landed one commit on a **public** repository self-certify a round, which is precisely the bypass D-226's enforcement clause was written to close. Permission is both narrower than the second and independent of the first. |
| Why permission is stronger, not merely different | It is the authorisation the repository actually enforces for writes, it cannot be changed by the commenter, and it does not depend on who is asking. `author_association` is a derived display value; `write`/`admin` is the access itself. |
| Fails closed, per consumer | In the **gate**, an unreadable permission -- a 403, a rate limit, a renamed or deleted account, an unexpected response shape -- yields no permission, the round is not counted, and not counted is red. In `check-review-dispositions.sh` the two are *opposites*: an uncounted round makes that guard exit 0, so collapsing "cannot tell" into "not a writer" there would fail OPEN while claiming the reverse. It therefore distinguishes three outcomes -- may record, may not, cannot determine -- and **exits 1** on the third, naming the login. Both behaviours are pinned by a regression case, and each case is red against the implementation before it. |
| Regression coverage | `scripts/test-review-gate-counting.sh` and `scripts/test-check-review-dispositions.sh` both gain the pair this decision exists for: an account whose association is **`CONTRIBUTOR`** and whose permission is `admin` **is** counted (the private-membership case), while a genuine drive-by contributor -- same association, permission `read` -- is **not**. Plus `write` being sufficient, and an unreadable permission counting as nothing. `test-review-gate-counting.sh` now extracts **both** `rounds_on_head()` and `round_author_is_trusted()` from the workflow and fails if either is missing, so the suite cannot pass against a gate that has lost its authorisation check. |
| Residual weakness, recorded | Unchanged from D-226: the marker is body text, so a round is still **forgeable by someone who can already write to this repository**. Permission narrows *who*, not *what* the claim proves. The compensating control remains `check-review-dispositions.sh`, which requires the finding threads the marker claims. |
| Bootstrap exception, stated plainly | The pull request carrying this correction cannot itself be gated by the mechanism it repairs -- until it is on `main`, no agent round can be counted on any head. `independent-review` is not a required context on `main` (only `validate` is), so this is a gap in evidence rather than a bypass of a required check, and it is recorded here rather than left implicit. Codex was quota-exhausted throughout (R-009), so the review was performed by read-only reviewer agents under D-226 -- four rounds, which found among other things that this branch's own live probe died silently on a 403. The round is recorded on the pull request BEFORE it merges, not by this row: a decision record must not assert evidence that does not yet exist, which is the failure class D-226 exists to close. |
| Rollback | Revert the adopting merge commit. The workflow, `validate_phase0.py` and `check-review-dispositions.sh` return to the `author_association` filter, and the gate returns to counting zero agent rounds. No data migration, no state to unwind. |
| Evidence | Measured on this repository: unauthenticated `GET /repos/workin-hr/hr-platform/issues/195/comments` reports `author_association = CONTRIBUTOR` for comment `5634205151`, whose author holds `admin`; the same comment reports `MEMBER` to the owner's token. Gate run `34597413154`, re-run after the comment existed, logged `0 round(s) on this head` with every other rule satisfied. `gh api orgs/workin-hr/public_members/karimtismail` returns 404 (membership private). Both gate suites pass with the new cases; `validate_phase0.py` 148/148. |

## D-227: The Backend Image Is Published Privately And Consumed By Client Developers

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **Accepted 2026-09-10 by the repository owner.** Recorded because #186 established an operational model the accepted-decision history did not otherwise carry: a published backend image, private, followed by a moving tag, with client developers as its consumers. |
| Decision | CI publishes `deploy/Dockerfile`'s image to GHCR on every push to `main` that touches the backend. Two tags: `:main`, which `deploy/compose.dev.yaml` follows, and an immutable `sha-<commit>`. Client developers pull rather than build, so a Flutter or desktop developer needs no JDK, database, credentials or Gradle. |
| Why an image at all | The alternative is what preceded it: every client developer holds the whole repository and runs a four-minute Gradle build in Docker each time the backend moves. That cost is paid by people who are not backend developers and cannot debug it when it breaks. |
| Private, not public | The repository is public only because GitHub Team is not funded (Q3, D-223); the code is a product the owner intends to sell. A public image would hand out the built artefact regardless of the repository's visibility, so the package is private and each developer authenticates with **their own** `read:packages` token. A shared token authenticates as its owner, over-grants everything else that account can read, and cannot be revoked for one person. |
| What the moving tag may carry | `:main` is published **only** from `refs/heads/main`. `workflow_dispatch` accepts any ref and the checkout builds what it is given, so without that condition one manual run from a feature branch would distribute unmerged, unreviewed backend code to every client developer automatically. A dispatch from another ref still publishes its `sha-` tag, which is what the trigger exists for. |
| What `sha-` does and does not promise | It names a commit, not a byte-identical build: re-running the workflow at the same commit republishes the tag, and `deploy/Dockerfile` uses floating base-image tags and `apt-get`. Each run therefore records the **digest**, and the runbook documents pinning by digest for an exact rebuild. |
| Supply chain | Every action in the publishing workflow is pinned to a full commit SHA. The job holds `packages: write`, so a retargeted action tag would run unreviewed code with permission to replace the image everyone pulls. `scripts/validate_phase0.py` enforces the pinning repository-wide, in bare and quoted form, so this cannot regress quietly. |
| Architecture | `linux/amd64` only, built on a GitHub-hosted x86 runner and documented as a prerequisite. An arm64 manifest was considered and declined for now: the Gradle build would run under QEMU emulation on every publish, which is a real cost on the free Actions tier this repository is on. If ARM64 Linux hosts appear on the team, the manifest is the answer and the runbook's prerequisite note is where it changes. |
| Two compose stacks, held together mechanically | `compose.dev.yaml` is a copy of `compose.local.yaml` that pulls instead of building. Prose kept them in step and prose failed: the reseed command named the wrong file, so following it destroyed the other stack's volume. `scripts/check_compose_dev_parity.py` now permits exactly two differences -- project name, and build versus image -- and fails on anything else in either direction, including an intended difference disappearing. |
| Related | **D-223** (why the repository is public), **D-165**, `docs/operations/running-the-backend-for-client-developers.md`, `deploy/compose.dev.yaml`. |

## D-229: The Employee Edit Form Carries Every Column Its Save Writes

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-14 in the pull request closing #212, the first of the dashboard parity epic (#211); accepted when the repository owner merges it. The owner set the epic's order -- data safety before design -- and its target: look like PHP, keep the port's safeguards. |
| Decision | The employees page's edit form is filled from `EmployeeStore.editForm`, which reads the stored columns and the latest shift assignment, and no longer from `Employee`, the list's display row. It has an input for every column `save_edit` writes, pre-filled and preselected: first and last name, code, phone, country code, national ID, birth date, gender, hire date, address, branch, department, job title, contract duration in legacy's months-or-years form (`employee_contract_form_values()`), and mobile attendance. The shift and its effective date are pre-filled too. **A save that changes nothing leaves the employee row and its shift assignments as they were.** |
| The defect | `EmployeeStore.update` writes fifteen columns from the post on every edit, and the form was filled from the list row. As a result: `first_name` carried the joined display name; `last_name`, `national_id` and `address` rendered empty; birth date, gender, contract duration and mobile attendance had no input; no select was preselected; and the hire date fell back to `created_at`. The save was refused until a branch was chosen again. Once it was, the save cleared six columns, turned mobile attendance off and wrote the full name into `first_name`. `compose.remote-db.yaml` enables admin actions against an existing database (**D-207**), so real data could reach this path. |
| Where it deliberately differs from legacy | Three places. In each, legacy's own form rewrites data on a save that changed nothing. **Hire date:** a missing one stays blank and is saved as missing, where legacy fills in today. **Gender `other`:** the column allows it but legacy's select does not offer it, so legacy clears it; the port offers "Other" only to an employee who already has it. **Deactivated org rows:** legacy lists only active branches, departments and job titles. An employee whose department or job title was deactivated after being set loses it on save, and one whose branch was deactivated cannot be saved at all. The port also lists the row the employee already has. `EmployeeAdminService` accepts that one row while inactive, still only within the employee's own company (**D-176**). A deactivated row can be kept, never newly chosen. |
| Only what changed is checked and written | Codex found these on the pull request. They are one class: an edit re-checked and rewrote values nobody had touched. **Unchanged values are not re-validated.** A code is validated only when it is replaced. Every one of the development seed's 3,783 employees has a code such as `E000002`, which the digits-only rule refuses, so no seeded employee could be saved at all. The code input carries the digits-only `pattern` only when the stored code already matches it, and an employee stored without a code keeps having none. A phone and its country code are validated only when either one is replaced. `join_company.php` stores a phone with no country code (**R-019**); the seed has 1,284 such rows, and the rule refuses that pair. A replaced code or phone is checked as before, and the add form still requires a valid code. **Unchanged columns are not written.** The update sets only the columns whose value differs from the stored row. Values are compared after trimming, with blank and NULL treated alike, so an unchanged save leaves padding, an empty string, and a country code beside a blank phone exactly as stored. **Zero dates:** legacy data holds MariaDB's `0000-00-00`; the seed has 68. No date input can hold that value, so a browser submits it as empty. An empty birth or hire date over such a value keeps it. The same shift with such a start date left empty adds no assignment. A date typed over one replaces it. Columns are left out of the `UPDATE`, rather than written back with their stored value, which also works under a strict `sql_mode`. Legacy's form re-validates and rewrites every column. There, these employees cannot be saved, or an unchanged save rewrites them. |
| Kept as legacy has it | **Contract duration:** the input keeps legacy's `min="1" max="60"`. A browser will not submit a stored duration over sixty months that is not whole years until it is changed. That blocks the save but loses nothing. **Inactive shift:** it is not listed, so the select posts none and the save leaves the assignment alone. **Add form:** it gains the same inputs, with mobile attendance ticked by default, as legacy's is. |
| Not in scope | The form's layout is **#216**: legacy's sections, the country-code select, the org cascade and the required markers. The salary contract is out of scope too; neither form edits it. |
| Regression coverage | `AdminEmployeesEndToEndTest` reads the rendered form as a browser would submit it and posts it back unchanged, for three employees: one fully populated; one with no hire date, gender `other`, an eighteen-month contract and attendance off; and one whose branch, department and job title were deactivated after being set. Each test asserts that the row and the latest assignment are unchanged, and that the save was accepted and audited. The audit check matters because a refused save also leaves the row unchanged. Two further tests pin that a deactivated department is neither listed nor accepted as a new choice, and that the add form ticks mobile attendance. Against the code before the fix, the two unchanged-save tests that existed then were both refused with `error_required`, and the add form saved attendance as `0`. **For the values the form cannot show,** the form reader also behaves as a browser does in two more ways: it submits a date input holding no valid date as empty, and it refuses a required field left empty. Five further tests use it: an employee with no code, a zero birth date beside a zero shift start date, and a zero hire date, each saved unchanged; a code the employee has cannot be blanked; and a date typed over a zero date is written. Before that fix, the no-code employee's form could not be submitted. The zero birth date was saved as NULL, with a new assignment dated from the hire date, and the zero hire date was saved as NULL. **For values an edit did not change,** the form reader also refuses a value its `pattern` does not match and a number outside `min` and `max`. Five more tests cover this. A code such as `E000002` and a phone stored with no country code are each saved unchanged. A replaced code is still refused by the digits rule, and a replaced phone is still refused without a country code. An employee with padded text, an empty national ID and gender, and a country code beside a blank phone is saved unchanged. Before that fix, the `E000002` form could not be submitted and the phone was refused with `error_required`. The padded employee's address was trimmed and their country code cleared. |
| Rollback | Revert the merge. The form returns to clearing data on save. Nothing is stored differently, so there is nothing to unwind. |
| Related | **#211**, **#212**, **#216**, **D-176**, **D-195**, **D-207**, **R-051**, **R-053**, **R-055**. |

## D-230: A Banner's WhatsApp Number Is Split Back Into Its Parts For Editing

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-14 in the pull request for #213's banners item; accepted when the repository owner merges it. |
| Decision | The banners edit form fills its WhatsApp country-code and number inputs from the stored `button_action_value`. It splits the value the way legacy's `banner_split_whatsapp_digits()` does: on the longest active dial code the digits start with, falling back to `+20` with every digit as the local number. For a WhatsApp button, the action-value input stays empty, as it does in legacy's edit form. **A save whose country code and number are unchanged from that split keeps the stored value as it is, provided legacy would store that value unchanged: eight to fifteen digits and nothing else.** Any other stored value is rebuilt from its parts. A rebuilt number follows `banner_normalize_whatsapp_phone()`: outside eight to fifteen digits it is no number, and is stored as NULL. |
| The defect | The button stores one string of digits, the dial code and local number together, and the form edits it as two inputs, which the edit form rendered empty. `BannerForm.whatsappNumber()` reads an empty number as no number. So saving an unchanged WhatsApp banner stored `button_action_value = NULL`: the button stayed, with nothing behind it. |
| Where it deliberately differs from legacy | Some stored numbers match no active dial code: the country was deactivated later, or the number predates the list. Such a number splits into `+20` plus every digit. On an unchanged save, legacy rebuilds it from those parts after passing the country code through `company_resolve_country_code()`. That puts `20` in front, or the first active dial code when other codes are active but `+20` is not. The rebuilt number then goes through `banner_normalize_whatsapp_phone()`, so a number the prefix makes longer than fifteen digits is stored as NULL and the link is lost: `44123456789012` becomes the sixteen-digit `2044123456789012`. The port keeps the stored value in every one of these cases, because the parts came back exactly as they were shown. A number that was actually changed is still built from its parts. **A stored value that is not an eight-to-fifteen-digit number is rebuilt, as legacy rebuilds it:** `+966 50-123-4567` becomes `966501234567`, and `javascript:alert(1)` or a seven-digit `2012345` becomes NULL. Keeping those would carry an unchecked value past the WhatsApp rule, and `banners/list` serves the value to the clients unsanitised. The independent review of `990637c1` found the keep rule keeping them. Checking that finding exposed the missing length rule behind it: rebuilt without it, `javascript:alert(1)` came out as `201`. The review of `180ce8ab` found that this row first said legacy always puts `20` in front of an unmatched number. It was corrected under **#223**. |
| Not in scope | Legacy resolves the country code through `company_resolve_country_code()`, and `BannerForm` uses the code as typed. That is left to its own change. The form's layout, including legacy's country-code select, is **#218**. |
| Regression coverage | `AdminBannersEndToEndTest` reads the edit form as a browser submits it, posts it back as multipart with the empty file part included, and asserts the save was accepted and audited. It covers five cases. An unchanged WhatsApp banner keeps its number. The form splits a stored number on the longest active dial code (`+966` rather than a seeded `+96`), with the action value empty. An unchanged number that matches no active dial code is kept. A changed number is written from its parts. An external-URL banner saved unchanged keeps its URL. `BannerFormTest` pins the split on its own: the longest code wins, non-digits are stripped, the `+20` fallback applies with or without codes, and a matched number recombines to exactly the stored digits. **Before the fix** (the changed files taken from `cfa0f08a`), 4 of the 5 end-to-end tests failed. Both unchanged WhatsApp saves stored NULL. The form's country code rendered empty. A changed number was saved without its dial code. The external-URL guard passed. **Mutants:** each part of the fix was switched off in turn, and each time its own test failed. Without the keep rule, the unmatched number was lost. With the action value shown, or without the longest-first sort, the split test failed. With the keep rule always applied, a changed number was not written. Without the country code prefilled, the unchanged save failed. **Round 1 (`990637c1`)** added five end-to-end tests and one unit test. A formatted stored number is rebuilt to digits. A stored value that is not a number, such as `javascript:alert(1)`, is not kept, and neither is a seven-digit `2012345`. An internal-route banner changed to WhatsApp with no number stores NULL. A banner with a leftover digits-only value, changed to WhatsApp, has its number built from its parts. `whatsappNumber()` returns no number outside eight to fifteen digits. With `BannerForm` and `BannerAdminService` taken from `990637c1`, four of these failed: the save kept `2012345`, `+966 50-123-4567` and `javascript:alert(1)`. Mutants: without the storable-number check, the three not-a-number tests failed. Without the stored-type guard, the leftover-digits test failed. Without both, the internal-route test failed as well. Without the length rule, the short-number, not-a-number and unit length tests failed. |
| Rollback | Revert the merge. The edit form goes back to clearing the number on save. Nothing is stored differently, so there is nothing to unwind. |
| Related | **#211**, **#213**, **#218**, **D-210** (the edit form this page gained), **D-229** (the same class of defect on the employees page). |

## D-231: A Row Dialog Sets A Checkbox From The Row

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-14 in the pull request for #213's faqs and phone_countries items; accepted when the repository owner merges it. |
| Decision | `row-dialog.js` ticks a checkbox that declares `data-dialog-field` when the row's trigger carries `"1"` for that field, and unticks it otherwise. It leaves the checkbox's `value` attribute alone, because that is what a ticked box submits. The faqs category and question edit dialogs and the phone-countries edit dialog declare `data-dialog-field="isActive"` on their Active checkbox, which renders unticked, and their triggers carry `data-dialog-isActive` as `"1"` or `"0"`. The add forms still start ticked, as legacy's do. |
| The defect | The three edit dialogs rendered the Active checkbox ticked and never filled it: the script wrote only values and text. `form.reset()` restored the tick each time a dialog opened. So saving an inactive category, question or country from its dialog, for example to correct its name, switched it back on. Legacy's edit modals set the box from the row (`faqs/page.php:260` and `:274`, `phone_countries/page.php:198`). |
| Why the row always carries `"1"` or `"0"` | A trigger with no value for a field leaves that field as the form rendered it. An attribute that jte omitted when false would have read as no value, so an inactive row would have taken the rendered default instead of its own state. |
| Swept | Every checkbox in the admin templates. Only these three dialogs fill a checkbox through `row-dialog.js`. `guide-videos.jte` renders each row's own edit form with `checked="${row.active()}"`. `banners.jte`, `employees.jte` and `departments.jte` set `checked` from the row being edited. Login's remember-me box and the notifications broadcast confirmation hold no stored state. |
| Regression coverage | **`AdminActiveCheckboxEndToEndTest`** renders each page, fills the row's dialog by the script's rules, posts it as a browser does and reads the row back. An active and an inactive category, question and country each keep their state when saved unchanged, and the dialog carries the row's other values. The add forms still start ticked. **Before the fix** (`faqs.jte` and `phone-countries.jte` taken from `320e417e`), 3 of the 4 tests failed: the inactive category, question and country were each re-activated. The add-form test passed. **Mutants:** without the triggers' `data-dialog-isActive`, and separately without the checkboxes' `data-dialog-field`, the same three tests failed, each with the active row switched off. **`deploy/e2e/tests/row-dialog.spec.js`** loads the real `row-dialog.js` onto a static page in Chromium. A row carrying `"1"` opens its dialog ticked and one carrying `"0"` unticked; the checkbox keeps `value="1"`; and a row with no value leaves the box as rendered, after the previous row's tick is reset. With `row-dialog.js` taken from `320e417e`, 2 of its 3 tests failed. With the checkbox always ticked, the inactive-row test failed. The spec needs no stack and runs with `npx playwright test --project=browser`. The end-to-end suite is not wired into CI, so CI runs the Java test and the spec is run by hand, with the rest of `deploy/e2e`. |
| Rollback | Revert the merge. Nothing is stored differently, so there is nothing to unwind. |
| Related | **#211**, **#213**, **D-210** (the edit dialogs these pages gained), **D-229** and **D-230** (the same class of defect: an edit form that does not carry back what its save writes). |

## D-232: The Setting Templates Tab Renders What Its Script Reads

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-14 in the pull request for #213's setting templates item; accepted when the repository owner merges it. |
| Decision | The tab keeps legacy's `setting-templates.js` and renders what the script reads. The hidden field takes legacy's id, `settingOptionDefId`. The value hint and the locked-value hint are rendered. The option dialog carries its two titles as `data-label-add` and `data-label-edit`. An option that companies use gets legacy's Delete, which shows the refusal with its company count instead of posting. The script now reads each value from an attribute of its own, where legacy passes one JSON attribute per button. It reads the titles from the dialog, where legacy sets them in an inline script. The in-use flag is written as `"true"` or `"false"`. |
| The defect | From the first port (`90633587`), the tab renamed the hidden field and rendered each value as its own attribute, while the script still looked for legacy's id and a JSON attribute. So "Edit definition" opened with every field blank. "Add option" and "Edit option" threw a TypeError before their dialog opened, because the script wrote into a field that was not there. Both option titles stayed in English on an Arabic page, and neither hint was rendered. |
| Why attributes rather than the JSON | jte escapes each attribute value itself. A JSON payload would need a JSON encoder in the view on top of that escaping. The port renders no inline script on any page, so the titles moved into the markup too. |
| Swept | Every admin script against every template, for element ids and data attributes a script reads that no template renders. Only this script was both loaded and broken. `account-menu.js`, `org-filter-cascade.js`, `phone-form-bind.js` and `request-filter-cascade.js` are copied but no page loads them. `crud.js` checks for its missing title attribute before using it. The elements `login.js` looks for and does not find belong to company and HR sign-in, which is **#220**. |
| Regression coverage | **`AdminSettingsEndToEndTest`** gains two tests. `theTemplatesTabRendersEveryElementAndAttributeItsScriptReads` renders the tab and reads `setting-templates.js` from the source tree. Every id the script looks up, and every data attribute it reads, must be on the page. It reads only literal names, so a name the script built at run time would pass unchecked. `anOptionsEditButtonCarriesTheRowItsDialogShows` checks that an option's edit button carries its row and its in-use flag, for both states, and that the Delete for an option in use carries its company count. **Before the fix** (the template and script taken from `320e417e`), both failed. **Mutants:** with the hidden field renamed back, or without `data-label-add`, the first test failed. With the in-use flag rendered as a jte boolean, the second failed. Without the explaining Delete, both failed. **`deploy/e2e/tests/setting-templates.spec.js`** loads the real script onto a page shaped like the tab, in Chromium. The definition dialog fills from its button. Add and edit open under the page's own titles. An unused value stays editable, and a value in use is locked. Delete on an option in use shows the refusal. No case may leave a page error. With `setting-templates.js` from `27123219`, four of the five cases failed. With the in-use flag read by presence, the unused-option case failed. The spec needs no stack; like `row-dialog.spec.js`, it runs by hand with `npx playwright test --project=browser`, and CI runs the Java tests. **Round 1 (`d0249321`)** found that Delete on an option in use left its row menu open: that branch keeps the click from reaching `row-actions.js` and, unlike the add and edit branches, did not ask it to close the menu. It now does. `delete on an option in use closes the row menu it came from` fails with the script from `d0249321`. The same round noted that the element test is page-wide, so the option button's own labels and sort order are now asserted too. Without `data-sort-order` on that button, `anOptionsEditButtonCarriesTheRowItsDialogShows` fails while the page-wide test still passes. |
| Not in scope | Legacy also shows each definition's description under its title, and an in-use warning as the usage badge's tooltip. Both are layout, left to **#218**. |
| Rollback | Revert the merge. Nothing is stored differently, so there is nothing to unwind. |
| Related | **#211**, **#213**, **#220**, **D-231** (the same kind of break between a script and the markup it fills, on the row dialogs). |

## D-233: An Advance's Row Menu Offers What Its Status Allows

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-14 in the pull request for #213's advances item; accepted when the repository owner merges it. |
| Decision | The advances row menu follows legacy's `hr_advances_row_actions()` (`hr_list_helper.php:763-838`). **Edit** and **Delete** appear while there is something to change: a pending advance, or an approved one with a balance still owed. Then **Approve** and **Reject** appear for a pending advance, or **Mark paid** for an approved one still owed. A rejected advance, or an approved one fully repaid, offers **Delete** alone. Mark paid carries legacy's `mark_paid` label. |

It offered Edit only for a pending advance, so an approved advance still owed could not be corrected from the page, although the service's edit handles that case (`editingAnApprovedAdvanceKeepsWhatWasAlreadyRepaid`). |

It renders the page and reads each row's menu in order: a dialog trigger by its dialog, a form by its action. It also checks that Mark paid carries the `mark_paid` label, in whichever language the page renders, and no longer a balance. **Before the fix** (`advances.jte` taken from `27123219`), it failed: the pending row offered Edit, Approve, Reject, Mark paid and Delete. **Mutants:** with Edit for a pending advance only, the owed row lacked Edit. With Mark paid for every approved or rejected row, the repaid row offered it. With the old label, the label check failed. Each run restored the template byte-identical. |

| Related | **#211**, **#213**, **D-210** (the edit dialog this page gained). |

## D-241: The Advance, Asset And Penalty Forms Search Every Active Employee, And An Edit Keeps Its Row's Employee

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-15 in the pull request for #214's searchable-picker item, for advances, assets and penalties. It is accepted when the repository owner merges it. |
| Decision | On these three pages, the add form and the edit dialog choose an employee with legacy's searchable picker (`emp-picker`), not a `<select>`. You type to filter by name or code, and up to 40 matches show. A label reads "name (code)", plus " — company" when no company is chosen, as in legacy's `hr_employee_option_label`. The list holds every active employee the page covers. The 500-row cap on the unfiltered list is gone, because legacy's `hr_employees_for_admin` has none. An edit keeps its row's employee even when the list no longer holds them, and shows the row's own label, as legacy's `advanceOpenEdit` does. |
| The defect | Each edit dialog set a `<select>` of active employees to the row's employee id. A deactivated employee had no option, so the required select stayed empty and the edit could not be saved. Codex found this on #233, and it was already true on `main` for every editable row on these three pages. With no company chosen, the select also stopped at 500 employees, so the rest could not be chosen at all. |
| How it works | **Markup:** `employeePicker.jte`. **Behaviour:** `emp-picker.js`. **Data:** `EmployeePicker` builds the labels and the page's list, rendered once per page as JSON in a `data-employees` attribute and shared by both pickers. **Row dialogs:** `row-dialog.js` now dispatches `row-dialog:filled` once it has filled a dialog, so the picker redraws from the row's id and label. **Safeguards:** the browser stops a submit with no employee chosen and marks the picker invalid, while a dialog's Cancel still closes. Enter in the search box never submits: it chooses the listed match when exactly one is listed. Enter in a search box should choose an employee, not submit a half-typed search. *Superseded reason:* when this was decided, a row dialog's first submit button was Cancel, so an Enter that submitted also closed the dialog and lost the edit. D-243 has since made Save the only submit button. The server's checks are unchanged: it refuses a missing employee, or one from another company. |
| Size of the page | The list goes into the page once, as an escaped JSON attribute. One entry takes about 180 bytes with Latin names and 240 with Arabic names. That was measured on representative entries under jte's attribute escaping. `LeaveBalanceStore` records 3,783 active employees on the platform. At that count, a page with no company chosen carries roughly 670–890 KiB of list. **Corrected by D-244:** that figure was read off a comment rather than measured, the comment is gone, and 670–890 KiB is an upper bound, not a measurement. With a company chosen, it carries only that company's employees. Legacy renders the same uncapped list into the same pages (`hr_employees_picker_list`), so this matches what production serves today. It is the cost of the owner's decision that the picker cover every active employee. If it proves too heavy, the fix is a search endpoint, not the cap back. |
| Not in this change | The leave balance and attendance add forms keep their selects; they move to the picker in their own change. Until then, leave balances keeps its 500 cap. The server still accepts an employee of the row's company whether active or not, as legacy does. |
| Regression coverage | **Java, per page** (`AdminAdvancesEndToEndTest`, `AdminAssetsEndToEndTest`, `AdminPenaltiesEndToEndTest`), two tests each. `anEditKeepsItsRowsEmployeeAfterThatEmployeeIsDeactivated` checks that Edit carries the row's id and legacy's label, the dialog holds a picker the row fills, the list leaves the deactivated employee out, and saving keeps them. `thePickerListsEveryActiveEmployeeUnderLegacysLabels` adds 520 employees and checks that the unfiltered list holds all 522 active, and that a label names the company only when no company is chosen. With the three templates and stores from `main`, all six failed. Each mutant failed only its own tests: each store's cap put back (that page's list test, 500 of 522); the dialogs not filled from the row; Edit without the row's label; labels never naming the company. **Browser:** `emp-picker.spec.js` and `row-dialog.spec.js`'s *a filled dialog says so before it opens* pass 18 of 18, including *Enter in the search box chooses a single match and never submits*. Eight mutants of `emp-picker.js` and `row-dialog.js` each failed only their own case. The eighth removes the Enter handler (17 of 18). A focus check whose mutant nothing caught was removed. |
| Rollback | Revert the merge. Nothing stored changes. |
| Related | **#214**, **#213**, **#233**, **D-210**, **D-231**. |

## D-242: Branches, Shifts And Decisions Ask Which Company A New Row Belongs To

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-15 in the pull request for part of #213's *Adding without a company filter fails* item. It is accepted when the repository owner merges it. |
| Decision | With no company filter chosen, the add forms for branches, shifts and administrative decisions show a required company select of the active companies. Legacy's `org_render_company_field_in_form` does the same, fed by `org_active_companies()`. A page already filtered to a company, or a session scoped to one, still sends that company hidden. Choosing a company there also needs legacy's cascade (`org-filter-cascade.js` and the per-page form scripts). Those four follow with that cascade. `PayrollStore.activeCompanies()` keeps its own copy of the query for now. |

With no company filter, the add form must carry a required company select that lists both active companies, leaves out a suspended one and posts no company of 0. A page filtered to a company must keep that company as a hidden input, with no select. With the templates and controllers from `main`, all three failed at "the add form asks for one". Each mutant failed all three at its own assertion: every company listed, not only active ones; the select not required; a filtered page asking anyway. |

## D-243: A Row Dialog's Cancel Is A Button, So Enter In A Field Saves

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-15 in the pull request that follows #236's review. It is accepted when the repository owner merges it. |
| Decision | In `rowDialog.jte`, Cancel is a plain button (`type="button"`, `data-dialog-close`) that `row-dialog.js` closes the dialog with. Save is the form's only submit button. Enter in a single-line field of a row dialog therefore submits through Save, as it does in legacy's modals, which have no submit button but Save. |
| The defect | Cancel was a `formmethod="dialog"` submit button placed ahead of Save. A browser submits a form on Enter through its first submit button, so Enter in a single-line field of any row dialog closed the dialog and lost what had been typed. A textarea takes Enter as a new line and was never affected. That meant 13 dialogs on 11 pages: advances, assets, attendance, companies, company detail, complaints, faqs, leave balances, penalties, phone countries and requests. #236's first review and Codex found it through the employee search box. #236 stopped Enter in that one box from submitting; this change fixes the cause for every field. |
| Why not reorder the buttons | Putting Save first in the markup and showing Cancel first with CSS `order` would also fix Enter, but it would make keyboard focus order differ from the visible order. A hidden default submit button is handled inconsistently across browsers. |
| What it supersedes | D-241 explains the picker's Enter handling by saying a row dialog's first submit button is Cancel. After this change that is no longer true. The picker keeps the handler for its own reason: Enter in a search box chooses an employee, and must not submit a half-typed search. `emp-picker.js`'s comment now says so. Its check for a Cancel that submits is removed, because no Cancel submits any more. |
| Regression coverage | **`AdminRowDialogButtonsTest`**, new. It reads `rowDialog.jte` with its comments stripped and requires exactly one submit button, Cancel as a `data-dialog-close` button, and no `formmethod="dialog"`. With `main`'s template it failed, finding 2 submit buttons. **Browser:** `row-dialog.spec.js` builds a page with the template's new shape. A new case, *Enter in a field submits the dialog through Save, and Cancel closes without submitting*, presses Enter in a field and then clicks Cancel. The `browser` project passes 10 of 10. With `main`'s `row-dialog.js`, all four `row-dialog.spec.js` cases failed, because each clicks Cancel, which that script does not close. `AdminAdvancesEndToEndTest`, whose page renders two row dialogs, and the four template gates pass. **On `main` with #236:** `emp-picker.spec.js`'s page now uses the same Cancel button, and its *cancel still closes* case now expects no submit at all. After the rebase the `browser` project passes 19 of 19: 8 picker, 5 row-dialog and 6 setting-templates cases. The picker spec's submit recorder stops every POST, with no exception for a Cancel that submits, so a submitting Cancel put back would fail its *cancel still closes* case. |
| Rollback | Revert the merge. Nothing stored changes. |
| Related | **#236**, **#214**, **D-241**, **D-231**. |

## D-236: Rejecting A Request Opens A Dialog With An Optional Reply

| Field | Value |
