## D-276: Both Notifications Writes Honour The Session, And The Gate Checks Per Method

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | Proposed 2026-09-23; accepted when the repository owner merges it. |
| Decision | **Both of the notifications page's writes honour the session's company, as legacy's do.** Three rules, all of them legacy's. (1) **The delete.** A session scoped to one company may delete only that company's row: `page.php:59-69` runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM notifications WHERE id=? AND company_id=?` when `$isComp`, flashes `error_db` and redirects on no match, and otherwise deletes by id. `BroadcastStore.companyOf(id)` is the ownership lookup and the service compares it against the session. (2) **The broadcast's target.** A scoped session with no posted company writes to its own (`helper.php:329-330`), and one naming a different company is **refused rather than retargeted** (`:331-332`). (3) **The broadcast's reach.** The all-employees audiences require `$isAdmin` (`:336-350`), so a scoped session cannot address past its own company. Both refusals on the send use `error_required`, which is what legacy's page flashes for a refused dispatch. An administrator *filtered* to one company with `?company_id=` is **not** scoped on any of the three -- the filter is a view, the scope is who you are -- so the platform's own capability is untouched. |
| Why | The delete was the one write on this surface that reached a tenant-owned row without resolving that row's company, which is why it was the one entry in `AdminTenantGuardCoverageTest.DELIBERATELY_CROSS_TENANT`. **The first commit of this branch fixed that and left its sibling**, which is the habit this repository keeps paying for: the broadcast took its `company_id` straight from a `@RequestParam` and checked only that the company existed. The review round found it, and found the worse consequence -- see the next row. **Nothing is exploitable today**: `AdminViewModelAdvice#session` returns `DashboardSession.admin` unconditionally, so every session this surface issues is a platform administrator's, and an administrator reaching every company is the page. All three rules are written now because afterwards their absence looks like the page working: R-044 rates this High precisely because the failure is silent. |
| The gate could not have caught it | Rule two of `AdminTenantGuardCoverageTest` asked whether a service's **source** mentioned `DashboardSession` anywhere. One guarded method satisfies that for every unguarded write in the same class -- so the moment the delete took a session, the broadcast fell out of **both** rules: rule one skipped it because its own signature took none, and rule two passed the whole class because the delete's did. Deleting the exemption at the same time, which the old rule's own self-policing demanded, removed the last written record that the gap existed. **Rule two is now per method**: every public service method that reaches a store method writing a tenant-owned table must take a session, following helpers the way rule one follows guards, because the write is often one level down. **54 write paths** are checked today -- counted, and re-counted by the delta reviewer -- and a regex that silently stopped matching fails the vacuity assertion instead of passing. The exemption list stays, keyed `Service::method` and empty: an empty allowlist is a stricter starting point than a missing one, and a per-method key cannot launder one method's guard into another's. **Two more laundering paths were still open and are closed here.** Rule one matched raw body text, so `session.companyId();` as a statement of its own passed -- it compares nothing and denies nobody -- and so did a mention inside a comment: the R-046 shape the gate exists to catch, satisfied by naming it. Comments and string literals are stripped now, and a guard whose result is thrown away does not count; the real tree's 58 session-taking methods all still pass, so no legitimate guard was a bare statement. And rule two's own new call-walk required `name(`, so a write behind `ids.forEach(this::writeRow)` was invisible and its public method was never asked for a session -- `::name` reaches `name` now. Seven cases drive the two rules from sources written to fail, including both laundering shapes, the method reference, and a paired case asserting the three shapes a real guard takes so the stricter rule cannot pass by refusing everything. |
| Also changed | `BroadcastAdminService`'s class javadoc claimed the audience "comes from a closed enum, never from a request-supplied company". The audience does; the company does not, and that sentence was the stated justification for the exemption this branch deleted. It now states all three legacy rules with their line numbers. `AdminNotificationsFlashTest` follows both new signatures and its five cases pin that the controller builds the session rather than the service inventing one. |
| Divergences from legacy | None. This is the opposite of a hardening: it restores three checks legacy has and the port dropped, reusing legacy's own `error_db` and `error_required` flashes rather than inventing keys. Two pre-existing divergences on this page are **not** touched, and are named so they are not mistaken for this change: legacy flashes `deleted_ok` even when the delete affected no row, where the port answers `error_not_found`; and legacy flashes `error_required` for a company that does not exist, where the port answers `error_not_found`. |
| Regression coverage | `AdminNotificationsTenantScopeTest`, **10 cases against a real MariaDB**, driven at the service because no HTTP session this surface issues can produce a scoped audience. The delete: another company's row refused with `error_db`, still present, no audit event; **its own company's row deleted**; an unscoped administrator deleting both companies' rows; a filtered administrator still deleting another's; a row that is gone refused on both arms. The broadcast: a scoped session naming no company reaching its own and only its own; a scoped session naming another company refused with nothing written for either; a scoped session refused the all-employees audience; **an administrator still reaching every company and still choosing one**; and a filtered administrator still choosing another's. Each "refuses" case is paired with the "still allowed" case that a refuse-everything guard would fail. **Eight mutants with a green control**, each dead on the test written for it: the own-company default removed, the refusal turned into a retarget, the all-employees check removed, the delete's ownership check removed, **rule two returned to its whole-file form**, rule one back to matching raw body text, the method reference back to invisible, and `used` refusing every guard -- the last one being the control for the strictness itself, since a refuse-everything bug would otherwise look like a working rule. One change here is deliberately **not** mutant-covered and is not claimed to be: moving the send's two refusals into legacy's order is unobservable, because both refuse with the same key and neither writes first. Suite: `AdminNotificationsTenantScopeTest` 10, `AdminTenantGuardCoverageTest` 13, `AdminNotificationsFlashTest` 5, `BroadcastStoreTest` 7 -- **35 tests, 0 failures**. |
| Rollback | Revert the two commits. No schema, no migration, no stored data changes; every behaviour that moves is a refusal on a path no session in production can currently take. An operator would see nothing. If a rule were wrong, the symptom would be a company-scoped user unable to delete or notify their own company, which is what the three paired "still allowed" cases assert. The gate change is test-only and reverting it costs coverage, not behaviour. |
| Review rounds | **Round 1**, a read-only `reviewer` agent in its own full clone on `6e307cd2`: `merge`, with one P2 and one P3 -- the P2 being that the first commit's own fix made the gate blind to the broadcast, and the P3 that the javadoc justifying the deleted exemption was false. It ran four mutants of the delete arm, all dead, and confirmed the legacy claim, the null handling, the ordering against the audit write and the absence of an existence leak by reading rather than by taking the body's word. Both findings are fixed above rather than deferred, together with the behavioural sibling neither of us had noticed until legacy's dispatch was traced. **Delta pass** on `32c51966`, same agent kind, own clone again: `clear` on all of it -- it re-derived the 54 write paths itself with a temporary print rather than trusting the assertion, re-ran all five mutants, verified the three legacy rules against `helper.php` and `page.php` itself, and confirmed the main merge brought in nothing foreign. It then found **three more**: rule one's named-guard laundering, rule two's blindness to a method reference, and my comment claiming legacy's order while the code had the other one. All three are fixed above. It also recorded one limitation it could not resolve and neither can this row: rule two cannot tell a propagated session from one a caller fabricated to satisfy a signature, which stays a review question rather than a gate one. |
| Related | **D-176** (the stored row's company decides, never the posted one), **R-044** (the silent failure this gate exists for), **R-046** (the legacy pages that write by row id unguarded), **ADR-0016** (the owner and HR logins that make all three rules live), **D-226**. |

## D-280: The Tenant Gate's Ground Truth Is The Whole Database, And Its Coverage Is Enumerated

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **ACCEPTED 2026-09-24.** An agent decision about a test, taken because the alternative is a security control that cannot say what it covers. No production code changes. |
| What was wrong | `AdminTenantGuardCoverageTest` is R-044's third mitigation -- the one that makes a missing tenant check fail the build rather than a review. It had two blind spots, and they compounded. **(1)** It derived "tenant-owned" from the vendored legacy schema alone, so the eight tables this repository declares itself in `src/main/resources/db/phase1-mysql` -- `attendance_devices`, `device_agents`, `device_punches`, `employee_device_identities`, `device_assignment_history`, `device_malformed_punches`, `device_operation_logs`, `legacy_refresh_tokens`, all carrying `company_id` or `employee_id`, all in the same MariaDB database -- were not tenant-owned as far as the gate was concerned. A write to any of them was unreviewable by construction. **(2)** Both rules select what to scan by name and location: `*AdminService.java`, or `<X>Store.java` beside an `<X>AdminService.java`, and only under the admin root. `LegacyPlatformAdminCompanyDirectory` writes `branches` from inside that root under a name matching neither pattern, so nothing scanned it. |
| What was **not** wrong | **No disclosure, and this matters for how the change is read.** All ten writers the rule now finds were traced, and the reasons are not one reason: the two `AttendanceDeviceStore` writes the admin surface reaches take an explicit `companyId` whose value its caller derives from the row (`DeviceAdministrationService.setActive` reads `device.companyId()` after `requireDevice`; `.allocate` reads `branchCompanyId(branchId)`), `update` making it a predicate and `claim`, an `INSERT`, the new row's column -- while its four other writes are `WHERE id = ?` and are not admin-session writes at all; `DeviceAssignmentHistoryStore` records a decision its caller already made; `LegacyCompanyDelete` deletes the company that *is* the operation's subject; the admin surface reaches `LegacyPayrollBatchStore` only through `PayrollAdminService`, whose **five** batch-write paths each take a `DashboardSession` (`createRun`, `finalizeRun`, `reopenRun` and `deleteRun` directly, `calculate` through `LegacyPayrollBatchService`'s connection-scoped copy; `editDetail` writes through `PayrollStore`, which rule two scans, and `actionsEnabled` and the static helpers write nothing), so rule one already guards it; `LegacyPlatformAdminCompanyDirectory.update` writes the main branch two ways and both are safe for a reason visible in the method rather than in the class javadoc (which is about not mutating the entity and says nothing about branches): the preceding `SELECT id FROM branches WHERE company_id = ? ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 1` resolves the id inside the company being edited, and when it finds nothing the `INSERT INTO branches (company_id, ...)` beside it writes that same company as a column (the if-branch, not the else-branch, as this row and the entry both said until the fifth round read the method). So this fixes a gap in a control, not a vulnerability, and the risk register says so rather than implying a breach. |
| Decision | **Two changes to the gate.** The ground truth becomes both halves of the database: `tenantOwnedTables()` reads `db/phase1-mysql/*.sql` by the same column test it applies to the vendored schema. And a **third rule** replaces the coverage assumption with an enumerated claim -- every class reachable from the admin surface that writes a tenant-owned table must be scanned by rule one or rule two, or named in `ACCOUNTED_FOR_OUTSIDE_THE_RULES` with the reason it is safe. |
| Why reachability, not "every writer in the repository" | Measured before choosing: at this head **68 files** contain a write to a tenant-owned table -- 59 by SQL text alone, 61 once a JPQL `@Modifying` write counts, 68 once a repository declared over a tenant-owned entity counts. Decomposed by predicate because a bare figure here was wrong twice for the same reason: it first said 120 write methods across 39 files, true of a narrower verb set and a half-database ground truth, and the correction said 61 -- measured minutes before the same commit taught the rule to count repositories, which added seven more. The fourth round caught the first, the fifth the second, and most belong to the legacy API, which has its own tenant control (`TenantFilterCoverageTest`, the tenant filter, `LegacyTenantContext`). Demanding an entry for each would produce exactly the wall of exemptions this test's own javadoc records rejecting once already, for the same reason: it would tell nobody anything. Scoped to what the admin surface can actually reach -- a transitive closure from the admin root outward -- the answer is **ten**. That is a list a person will read. |
| Why reach means code and not prose | The closure strips comments first, so a `{@link}` naming a store in a javadoc does not invent a call. Without that, the gate would demand a written reason for a class the admin surface only talks about, and unnecessary entries are how a list stops being read. **Removing the stripping changed no other assertion in the class**, so it was untested defence; `aClassNamedOnlyInACommentIsNotReached` asserts the property on the helper directly, which is what makes that mutant die. |
| The closure was wrong once, and the round caught it | **The first version of this rule claimed an exhaustiveness it did not have.** Its closure followed `import` statements and inline fully-qualified names -- and Java requires neither for a class in the same package, so `private final DeviceAgentStore agents;` is a real edge with nothing to match. Matching only those two shapes missed **every edge inside a package**. The review round reimplemented the closure independently, reproduced this change's own numbers (213 classes, 5 writers), then added same-package resolution and got **234 and 9**: `DeviceAgentStore` (`device_agents`), `DevicePunchStore` (`device_punches`), `EmployeeDeviceIdentityStore` (`employee_device_identities`) and `LegacyPayslipStore` (`payslips`) were all reachable, all writing a tenant-owned table, and all invisible. Reproduced here before being believed, and fixed. The resolution is deliberately narrow -- a bare capitalised word counts only against **this file's own siblings** -- because widened to every known simple name, a bare word in any file would invent an edge to anything sharing it. All four are safe, each for a reason now written down; none was a disclosure. The lesson is the one this whole entry is about: **a gate that names its own coverage can be wrong about it, and the only way to find out is for someone else to compute it.** |
| One reason was false as written | The round also found that the `AttendanceDeviceStore` entry claimed *"every write takes an explicit companyId and scopes by it"* -- and four of its six writes are `WHERE id = ?` with no company at all (`touchSeen`, `recordHandshake`, `recordSelfDescription`, `recordAttlogStamp`). They are sound, but not for the stated reason: their only callers are `DeviceAgentIngestService` and `ZkTecoAdmsService`, where the terminal has authenticated by serial or agent token and that identity resolved the row. Because rule three is per class, one entry covers a whole file's writes -- so a reason that overclaims misleads the next reader about writes it never examined. Corrected to name the two shapes separately -- and then corrected again by the second round, which found that the rewrite still attributed `WHERE company_id = ? AND id = ?` to `claim`, an `INSERT` with no `WHERE` at all. Sweeping the remaining eight entries for the same shape of error (the defect is a claim generalised across a group of methods, not a typo about one) found two more: `EmployeeDeviceIdentityStore` said every statement was scoped by the company when its `INSERT` writes the company as a column, and `LegacyCompanyDelete` said every statement was `WHERE company_id = ?` when several are predicated through an owning parent and the last is `DELETE FROM companies WHERE id = ?`. All three corrected, and `LegacyPayslipStore`'s entry, which both shifted subject from the store to the service mid-sentence *and* called an `INSERT` a row-id write, now says whose `create`/`update`/`delete` it means and which of the store's three writes carry a predicate. The lesson is recorded in the entry itself: an exemption's SQL shape has to be read off each method, because rule three is per class and one sentence then speaks for a whole file. |
| The write detector was wrong too, and the third round caught that | **The closure was only half the rule; the other half is knowing what a write looks like, and it knew three verbs.** `WRITE_STATEMENT` matched `INSERT INTO`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE FROM`. This repository also writes `INSERT IGNORE INTO` (the de-duplicated device ingest, `DeviceMalformedPunchStore` and `DeviceOperationLogStore`) and MySQL's multi-table `DELETE <alias> FROM` (eight files use one or the other), and it writes in JPQL through `@Modifying @Query`, which names the *entity* rather than the table -- so the pattern matched, compared `LegacyEmployee` against a set of table names, and reported that nothing was written. **This is worse than a narrow closure.** A writer the closure cannot reach is at least absent from the list; a writer the verb set cannot see is neither *found* nor *unaccounted for*, so no direction of the ratchet notices it and the gate reports full coverage of a set it never looked at. One writer was actually hidden this way: `DeviceMalformedPunchStore.quarantine`, `INSERT IGNORE INTO device_malformed_punches` -- a table this very change added to the ground truth -- reachable from the admin surface by the same file import as `DevicePunchStore`, and safe for the same reason (the company is `device.companyId()` off a resolved device). It is the tenth entry. The verb set now covers `INSERT [IGNORE] INTO`, `REPLACE INTO`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE [alias] FROM`, and a JPQL write is translated through an entity-to-table map read from the entities themselves; both are pinned by synthetic-source tests, because the previous version of this gap was invisible precisely for want of them. No JPA writer of a tenant-owned table is reachable from the admin surface today -- measured, not assumed, and now it cannot become so silently. |
| The ratchet asserts names, not a count | Also the round's: `isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(5)` was a dead ratchet -- loosening it to `>= 0` was caught by nothing, because nothing else re-derived the count. It now asserts the writer set **by name** against the map's keys, so a writer appearing *and* a writer quietly disappearing because the closure narrowed both fail, and the failure says which one moved. That second direction is exactly how the same-package gap hid four writers while the gate stayed green. |
| A third write category, found by the fourth round | **A repository write has no statement to find at all.** `interface LegacyBranchRepository extends JpaRepository<LegacyBranch, Long>` can write `branches` through `save`, `delete`, or a derived `deleteByIdAndCompanyId` whose SQL exists nowhere in the source -- and two such derived deletes are in this repository today. The javadoc added by the third round claimed this category was "handled"; it was not, because translating an entity name only helps a write that has *text*. Closed rather than documented: a repository declared over a tenant-owned entity now counts as a writer of that table, which takes `save`, `saveAll`, `delete`, `deleteAll` and every derived write at once -- reachability is by class reference, so a service injecting the repository in order to call `save` makes the repository reachable, and the repository is then a writer that must be scanned or accounted for. It over-approximates (a repository only ever read from still counts) in the safe direction: it can demand an exemption that was not needed, never hide a writer. It adds nobody today -- no repository of a tenant-owned entity is reachable from the admin surface -- which is exactly why it needed a test rather than a measurement. |
| Prose outlived the code twice more, and the seventh round widened the verb set again | **The sixth and seventh rounds found no hole in what the gate catches. They found the gate describing itself wrongly, which is the failure this whole entry is about.** Round 6: a new test had been inserted *between* an existing javadoc and the method that javadoc described, and Java binds only the last of two consecutive doc comments, so the paragraph carrying the 32-table figure documented nothing. Round 7 found the same shape a second time in the same file -- `JPA_REPOSITORY`'s 24-line javadoc was separated from its field by a one-line comment belonging to the next one -- plus two stale figures: this entry's *two writers* (six) and a claim that reverting the ground truth "still passes every other assertion", which it does not. It also found **two real detection gaps and one blind spot**. `INSERT IGNORE` was fixed in round 3 as itself rather than as a class, so `UPDATE IGNORE` -- one keyword from an idiom this repository already uses -- read the modifier *as the table name* and saw a write to nothing; and a schema-qualified `workin.employees` captured `workin`. Both are closed by `STATEMENT_MODIFIERS` and `SCHEMA_PREFIX`, each pinned by its own test. The blind spot is a **simple-name collision**: the index is keyed on a simple name with `putIfAbsent` and rule three skips by file name, so a second `EmployeeStore` deleting from `employees`, imported from the admin root, left `found` at ten and the build green. `noTwoClassesShareASimpleName` forbids the collision outright, and the same class renamed `WidgetStore` *is* caught by rule three -- which is what proves the name was the only thing hiding it. |
| The eighth round found a hole the seventh round's fix had opened | **The `SCHEMA_PREFIX` added above allowed whitespace around the qualifier's dot, and `Matcher.find()` resumes at the end of the previous match.** So a `-- comment sentence ending in a period.` sitting directly above a statement swallowed that statement's *verb* as the table name: `-- resolve the row first. Then update it.` above `DELETE FROM employees WHERE id = ?` yielded `DELETE`, and the write to `employees` was seen by nothing -- neither found nor unaccounted for. **That is the one direction this scan must never fail in, and the commit closing two such gaps opened a third.** The dot now takes no whitespace; a real qualified name never spaces it, and a spaced one costs at most an exemption. Reproduced as a failing assertion against the unfixed code before the fix, which is how it was confirmed rather than argued: the first reproduction attempt did *not* fail, because it put `jdbc.update(` between the comment and the SQL and the swallow ate `jdbc` instead of the verb -- the shape only bites when the verb is the first token after the period, as it is inside a SQL text block. The same round also falsified the other half of that sentence: a table named *exactly* like a modifier is read as the modifier, so `noTenantOwnedTableIsNamedLikeAStatementModifier` now checks that bound over both schema halves instead of describing it. Re-measured after the change, with an independent replica: **59** files write a tenant-owned table by SQL text under the old, the loose and the tight pattern alike, and no file differs between them, so the 68-file decomposition stands. |
| The ninth round found that the eighth round's fix had closed one instance of its own finding | **The separator was never the point: the tail was.** Because the pattern *consumed* the table token, `Matcher.find()` resumed past it, so whenever the word immediately before a statement's verb was itself a write verb -- prose included, no punctuation needed -- that statement's verb was captured as the table name and eaten, and its real table was never examined. `-- the caller already resolved the company, so this can safely update` above `DELETE FROM employees WHERE id = ?` yielded `[DELETE]`. **This half of the class predates round 7 entirely** -- the original three-verb pattern did it too -- and the eighth round's dot fix closed only the variant where a full stop supplied the separator, while the javadoc it shipped with asserted in bold that the dot was the whole of the reason. Nine comment lines under `com.workin` already end in a write verb (`DepartmentStore.java:228`, `PunchPairingStore.java:426` among them), and this repository's style puts `--` prose directly above the statement inside a SQL text block, so the shape is one plausible edit away rather than hypothetical. Closed by matching the table in a **lookahead**: the match ends at the verb, a wrong capture is additive, and nothing can hide behind it. With the tail no longer consuming, recognising more shapes became free, so the qualifier took back the spaced form the eighth round had made invisible -- whether MariaDB accepts `workin . employees` stops mattering, which is the right way for that question to be settled. The round also found that both schema readers kept a table's declared case while the scanner is case-insensitive, so a `CREATE TABLE Delayed` would have passed the modifier assertion and still been read as a modifier; the names are now lower-cased. Re-measured across all four pattern generations: **59** writer files each time, per-file table sets identical, so no figure moves. |
| The tenth round: the case fix landed in the dead copy of the scanner | **Three places compared a captured name against the table set, and the previous commit normalised two of them -- one being `servicesWritingTenantTables`, the unreferenced twin tracked as #335, while rule two's live collector went on comparing raw.** So the sentence above was false when written, and the gap was *introduced* by the fix: before it, the ground truth kept a table's declared case and the write side kept source case, so a table declared `Foo` and written `Foo` matched. Afterwards the ground truth was `foo` and rule two missed it. This schema half already ships upper-case `CREATE TABLE` (`SPRING_SESSION`, `SPRING_SESSION_ATTRIBUTES`), so the first upper-case-named table carrying `company_id` would have put rule two blind on it, and no assertion would have said so -- rule two's vacuity guard is a floor (`> 40`), not a count. Closed two ways: one named `canonical(...)` used at every comparison, so a raw one is visibly the odd one out, and **rule two now asks the same predicate rule three asks** rather than keeping a second copy -- verified behaviour-preserving by computing both collectors and asserting they are identical before switching. The round also corrected two claims in this file's javadocs that were wrong in the way rounds 7-9 were: the class-level argument said no match can consume another statement's verb, and `DELETE`'s alias slot does exactly that when a comment ends in `delete` (nothing is hidden, because the token after the consumed `FROM` is that statement's own table -- so the invariant is that no match *ends at or past* a table, which is what the javadoc now says); and the qualifier was called additive when it is greedy and replaces the capture. Two more: an assertion this change had made unfalsifiable now reads the raw `@Table` capture, and the modifier bound now covers entity names too, because a JPQL write puts the entity where the table goes. |
| What the gate still cannot see | Two shapes with a live example, each asserted by its own test -- and **not** a closed enumeration: #334 records the shapes review has named with nothing here to assert against (`TRUNCATE TABLE`, a multi-table `DELETE t1, t2 FROM`, an `UPDATE a JOIN b SET`, a tenant column added by a later `ALTER TABLE`, a repository reaching `JpaRepository` through an intermediate interface). The two below are: a statement whose table name is a variable (`"DELETE FROM " + table`) has no table name in its text. `LegacyCompanyDelete` writes **32** tables that way -- its four cascade lists -- and is on the list for its own reasons, so nothing is hidden today -- but a store whose *only* writes were of that shape would be invisible to rule three. Recorded here and asserted in `aTableNameBuiltFromAVariableIsNotSeenAndThatIsRecorded`, so it is a known limit rather than the next round's discovery. **The second is not a detection gap but a limit of what "tenant-owned" means here:** a table owned only through a non-employee parent carries neither tenant column, so the ground truth never calls it tenant-owned and no rule looks at a write to it. `department_branches` (through `departments`) and `company_setting_values` (through `company_settings`) are the live examples, and `DepartmentStore.syncBranches` writes the first with no company predicate. Nothing is hidden -- that store also writes `departments` and its service methods take a session -- but a store whose *only* write were of that shape would be invisible to all three rules and to the ratchet. Asserted by `aTableOwnedOnlyThroughItsParentIsNotInTheGroundTruth` and tracked as **#334**, because following a foreign key into a tenant-owned parent changes what this gate covers rather than how it looks, and that is its own decision. |
| Self-policing, in both directions | Like `DELIBERATELY_CROSS_TENANT` before it: an entry whose class stops writing a tenant-owned table, stops being reachable, or becomes scannable by rule one or two **fails** rather than outliving its reason. A new writer reaching the admin surface fails until someone writes the reason down. |
| Regression coverage | **Twenty-three mutants, all dead, against a green control of 30.** The tenth round's three: the shared predicate comparing the raw capture again (kills the case assertion, which now covers rule two as well because rule two uses that predicate); `@Table(name = "Employees")` on `LegacyEmployee` (kills `theEntityTableMapComesFromTheEntitiesThemselves`, which could not fail before this round); and an `@Entity class Delayed` mapped to `employees` (kills the extended modifier bound). The ninth round's two: the table matched by consumption instead of by lookahead (kills `aSchemaQualifiedWriteNamesItsTable`, which now pins the general shape rather than the full-stop instance), and a tenant-owned table named `Delayed` -- mixed case, the form that used to slip past -- added to the Phase 1 schema (kills `noTenantOwnedTableIsNamedLikeAStatementModifier` alone). The eighth round's two: the qualifier's dot allowed whitespace again (kills `aSchemaQualifiedWriteNamesItsTable`, whose sentence-boundary assertion is the regression test for the hole that introduced), and a tenant-owned table named `delayed` added to the Phase 1 schema (kills `noTenantOwnedTableIsNamedLikeAStatementModifier` alone). The seventh round's two: `WRITE_STATEMENT` restored to its pre-round-7 form (kills `aWriteVerbWearingAModifierIsStillAWrite` and `aSchemaQualifiedWriteNamesItsTable`, and nothing else -- which is also the evidence that widening it added no writer); and a second `EmployeeStore` under `devices/registry`, deleting from `employees` and imported from the admin root (kills `noTwoClassesShareASimpleName` alone, with rule three staying green -- the invisibility itself, reproduced). Its **red control**: the same class renamed `WidgetStore` fails rule three instead, so the collision was the only thing hiding the write. The fourth round's five: the repository rule disabled (kills `aRepositoryWriteWithNoStatementIsSeenThroughItsEntity`); `@Table`'s `name` required to be its first attribute again, and the same scan allowed to run past the annotation into a field called `name` (both kill `theTableNameIsFoundWhereverItSitsInTheAnnotation`, which exists because *coverage of today's entities cannot see a narrowing* -- all twelve write `name` first, so the coverage assertion stayed green through that mutant until this test was added); and the production scan wired to an empty entity map (kills `theProductionScanUsesTheRealEntityMap`, added because that one line -- the join between the map and the rule -- was covered by nothing, so this change's headline feature could be disconnected with every test still green). The earlier nine: The two added for the write detector: the verb set narrowed back to the original three (kills `theWriteDetectorSeesEveryVerbThisRepositoryUses` and, separately, rule three itself, which then reports `DeviceMalformedPunchStore` as a stale entry -- the ratchet catching the regression from the other direction), and the entity-to-table translation removed (kills `aJpqlWriteIsReadAsAWriteToTheEntitysTable`). The original seven: The Phase 1 schema read removed (kills two tests -- the ground-truth assertion, and rule three's ratchet, because **six** writers stop being writers when the tables they write stop counting: each of the six device stores writes exactly one Phase 1 table and nothing else, so `found` drops from ten to four and six entries are reported stale. This row said *two* until the seventh round measured it -- the figure was written when the list had five entries); one accounting entry deleted; a bogus entry added; the comment stripping removed. A fifth test names the eight tables explicitly so that reverting the ground truth cannot pass quietly. Then three more from the review round's findings: the same-package resolution removed (kills two -- the helper test and rule three itself), the sibling set widened to every known class, and one of the four new entries deleted. One mutant is deliberately *not* claimed: loosening the ratchet assertion itself survives, because an assertion cannot catch its own deletion -- that is a tautology rather than a gap, and saying so is better than implying coverage that cannot exist. One mutant first appeared to survive because the substitution did not apply -- the run was an unmutated tree -- which is why the harness aborts on a failed substitution and prints the line it changed. |
| Rollback | Revert the commit. Test-only: no production code, schema, migration or configuration changes. The risk if this were wrong is a gate that demands an exemption it should not, which fails the build loudly rather than passing something unsafe -- the safe direction for a control to err in. |
| Related | **R-044** (amended with this blind spot, and with the finding that it was not a disclosure), **D-176** (the invariant the guards implement), **D-276** (the last time a write slipped out of both rules, and the exemption that had documented it was deleted with the gap), **R-046**/**R-053**/**R-059**/**R-064** (the legacy instances of the invariant being missing), **D-164** (the Phase 1 device tables). |

## D-279: The Weekly-Rest Credit Asks About Leave Once Per Page, Not Once Per Workday

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **ACCEPTED 2026-09-23.** An agent decision, on the same footing as D-278: a defect in code this port wrote, with no legacy behaviour to preserve or diverge from. Every number the page prints is unchanged; only the count of statements that produce them moves. |
| Decision | **`attendance_is_on_approved_leave()` moves to `LegacyAttendanceCalendar`, which is where the PHP function lives and which is already `@RequestScope`, and gains a batched pre-warm beside the shift one.** `LegacyAttendanceCalendar.warmApprovedLeaveForEmployees` selects every approved paid-leave interval overlapping the window for every employee on the page in one statement and fills the cache `isOnApprovedLeave` consults. `LegacyWeeklyRestCredit.isOnApprovedLeave` is removed rather than left forwarding: its three callers -- that class's own `creditStatus`, `LegacyAttendancePeriodStats` and `LegacyAttendanceReportDetails` -- all already hold the calendar, so they ask it directly and the PHP-parity javadoc lives in one place instead of two. No test referenced the removed method. Four call sites warm: `AttendanceStore.aggregate`, `LegacyAttendancePeriodStats.employeePeriodStats`, and both of `LegacyAttendanceReportDetails`' per-date loops -- `absentDetails` and `voidWeeklyRestAbsentDetails`. The second of those was found by sweeping for siblings rather than by the measurement: it is the same per-date shape one method down, and a change that fixed only the method the budget test exercises would have left it. Both warm the *same* window, and the warm memoizes `(ids, from, to)` so a report calling both pays one statement, not two. **The memo records the window only after the query has filled it**: marked before, a warm whose query threw would leave the window marked with nothing cached, and every date in it would fall back to the per-date query for the rest of the request -- right answers, and the round trips this change exists to remove quietly back. Found by the second review round, which rated it P3 and unreachable today because all four call sites let the exception propagate; fixed anyway, because the reason it is unreachable is a property of the callers and not of this method. `aWarmWhoseQueryFailedIsNotRememberedAsDone` injects a failing connection and asserts the retry still queries. |
| The measurement | Counted with the existing `QueryCounter` against a company that takes Friday off -- this market's ordinary configuration, and the one D-278's fixture lacked. **Ten rows over a month: 286 statements before, 38 after**, and 240 of those 286 were `isOnApprovedLeave` alone. One row over a month: **34 before, 11 after**, which is now exactly what a week costs. At the remote stack's measured 106 ms per round trip that is ~30 s of round trips for a default page reduced to ~4 s. |
| Why the term was per row *and* per date | `weeklyRestDatesByStatus` walks every date of the period; on each weekly-rest date `creditStatus` walks the preceding workdays, and asks `isOnApprovedLeave` once for each. Friday off gives four or five rest dates a month and up to six preceding workdays each, so the count is rows x rest dates x workdays -- the shape D-278 removed for shifts and left standing here. |
| Why the overlap predicate is the same answer | The per-date query compares one date against `from_date`/`to_date`; a warm has to select rows for a *range*, so it selects by overlap (`from_date <= to AND to_date >= from`) and then re-decides each date with the per-date comparison. The overlap form cannot drop an interval the per-date query would have matched for a date in range, and the per-date re-check is what stops it adding one. **A date the warm did not reach falls back to the query rather than reading as "not on leave"** -- which matters because `creditStatus` walks up to fourteen days behind the period it was asked about, so callers warm a wider window than they report on. |
| Regression coverage | `LegacyApprovedLeaveWarmTest` compares the warmed answer against a **fresh** calendar's per-date query for every date of a month and three employees, and pins the shapes that decide it: an interval wholly inside the window, one beginning before it, one ending after it, ones wholly outside, both inclusive boundaries, a `pending` and a `rejected` request, and a request type with `counts_as_paid_leave = 0`. Two tests exist only for the fall-back: a date outside the warmed window, and an employee the warm was not given. Two more pin the memo, which no assertion about answers can see: the same window twice costs one statement, a different window costs two. **Eight mutants, all dead, against a green control**: the `from_date` day dropped, the `to_date` day dropped, the overlap predicate narrowed to containment, an absent cache key read as `false`, each of the two filters removed from the batch, the warmed window losing its last day, and the memo recorded before the query rather than after. The absent-key mutant is killed only by the two fall-back tests -- nothing else in the change sees it. **The last two came from the second review round, and the first round had claimed there was no surviving seventh**: a warm that walks its window with `date.isBefore(last)` drops the final day of every window and *every answer stays correct*, because an uncached date falls back to the per-date query. Only a statement count can see that, so `everyDateOfAWarmedWindowIsAnsweredWithoutAStatement` counts 62 lookups over a warmed month and requires zero statements. The round inferred that mutant from reading rather than running it; it was then run, and it did survive. `AttendanceAggregateQueryBudgetTest` grows a second fixture company with three rest-day rows, because the one-row fixture could not tell a per-row term from a per-date one, and its stale `<= 12` per-row bound tightens to the measured **9**. |
| A second, smaller read | `officialHolidaysWorkingDaysInRange` had its own uncached `company_official_holidays` read, issued once per row for a query whose arguments do not depend on the employee -- 10 statements of the 286. It now goes through `LegacyAttendanceCalendar.holidaysByDate`, whose memoized read has the identical `WHERE company_id = ? AND holiday_date BETWEEN ? AND ?`. It returns a date-keyed map where this read a row list, and **that is the same count only because `uq_company_holiday_date` makes `(company_id, holiday_date)` unique**: two rows on one date cannot exist to be collapsed. |
| The cost this adds | A company with **no** weekly rest day and no rest dates pays one extra statement for a warm it never reads: the no-rest fixture went from 22 to 20 for four rows, so the holiday saving covers it there, but the warm itself is +1. Measured, not assumed, and accepted against the 248 it removes for a normally-configured page. |
| Rollback | Revert the commit. No schema, no migration, no data change, and no change to any number the page prints. What an operator would see if this were wrong: a weekly rest day paid on the attendance report and unpaid on the payslip for the same employee and period, or the reverse -- the parity test is what makes that a build failure rather than a payroll dispute. The lexical date comparison is correct only while `requests.from_date` and `requests.to_date` are `DATE` columns; that dependency is stated in the method's javadoc, and `check_legacy_schema_drift.py` is what would catch a widening. |
| What is still per row | Three lookups inside `summarise`, 30 of the remaining 38 for a ten-row page: `approvedLeaveDays`, `employeeWorkHoursPerDay` and `attendanceFlagsInRange`. Each is one statement per row and none grows with the period, so the page's cost is now linear in rows and flat in days. Batching them means batched variants inside `LegacyPayrollAttendanceFigures`, which payroll shares, and is its own change. |
| Related | **D-278**, whose remaining term this closes, and whose "what is left" row named this work, and **D-099** (the session data source's own per-checkout statement, which is why the budget tests wrap a plain `DriverManagerDataSource`). |

## D-278: The Attendance Report Asks Once Per Page, Not Once Per Employee Per Day

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **ACCEPTED 2026-09-23.** An agent decision: this is a defect in code this port wrote, with no legacy behaviour to preserve or diverge from -- the numbers on the page are unchanged, only the number of statements that produce them. |
| Decision | **`AttendanceStore.aggregate` pre-warms the page's shifts and holiday credits before the per-row loop.** `LegacyAttendanceCalendar.warmShiftsForEmployees` resolves every employee on the page for every day of the period in one statement and fills the cache `shiftForEmployeeOnDate` already consults; `officialHolidayCreditForEmployees` does the same for the credit `summarise` asked per row. `summarise` itself is unchanged. |
| The measurement | Counted with the existing `QueryCounter`, not estimated. Three rows over a month: **109 statements, of which 90 were the per-employee-per-day shift query**; the same three rows over a week: 40. Ten rows over a month was **354**. At the remote stack's measured 106 ms per round trip that is ~37 s for a default page and minutes at `per_page=200`, which an operator reads as a hung page rather than a slow one. After: **18 for the same three rows, and a month costs exactly what a week costs** -- the committed fixture is four rows, one of them hired part-way through the period, and measures 22 over both a week and a month. |
| Why it was invisible | The cache that memoises the shift lookup is `@RequestScope`, so it is empty at the start of every request and the cost is paid on every request, not only the first. A harness that wires the collaborators once and measures twice reports the *second* request's warm cost -- 17 statements where a real request pays 109 -- so the budget test builds its collaborators per measurement. That is recorded because the first version of the test did it the other way and reported a number that looked fine. |
| Why not fix it in the figures classes | `weeklyRestDatesByStatus` and `expectedWorkDays` resolve the shift per date because that is what the PHP does, and payroll shares them. A pre-warm needs no change there at all: it fills the same cache those calls already hit, so the parity-critical arithmetic is untouched and the batch cannot answer differently from the query it replaces. |
| Why it is a pre-warm and not a second query | It selects the same columns, and the in-memory walk is the inverse of `ORDER BY effective_from DESC, esa.id DESC LIMIT 1`: dates walked forward, keeping the last assignment that has taken effect, and caching the `null` that a date before any assignment answers with so it is not re-asked. `LegacyAttendanceCalendarWarmTest` asserts the warmed value equals the per-date query's for **every date of the month and both employees**, plus the boundaries that decide it -- the day an assignment takes effect, the day before, and two assignments effective the same day where only `esa.id` separates them. |
| Regression coverage | `AttendanceAggregateQueryBudgetTest` ratchets both axes, because either alone can pass by accident: a month must cost exactly what a week costs (the rows-times-days term), and rows must cost a bounded amount each (**at most 12 statements for three extra rows**, which is the four per-row lookups that remain). A third case pins the {@code null}: an employee hired part-way through the period must cost what one assigned years ago costs, because the dates before their first assignment are answered from the warm rather than re-asked -- a mutant that cached only the non-null shifts passed every other test in the change, and this is the one that kills it. `AttendanceHolidayCreditBatchTest` asserts the batched credit equals the per-employee query's for every employee on the page, and the numbers the correlated `NOT EXISTS` decides -- a budget test alone would pass against a batch that counted the wrong thing. **Five mutants, all dead, against a green control of 49**; the review round ran eight of its own, seven dead and one surviving harmlessly (`put` for `putIfAbsent`, whose two values can only ever be equal -- the code now uses `put` and says why): the pre-warm removed, the same-day tie broken the other way, an assignment taking effect a day late, a date before any assignment not cached as null, and the credit back to one query per row. |
| What is left | Four lookups are still made per row inside `summarise` -- approved leave days, the employee's work hours, the attendance flags in range, and `expectedWorkDays`' own holiday read -- and **`LegacyWeeklyRestCredit.isOnApprovedLeave`, which the review round found does grow with the period**. An earlier revision of this row claimed the remainder "does not grow with the period"; that was true only of the budget fixture, which has `days_off = ''` and no `WEEKLY_OFF_DAYS` and therefore no rest dates at all. `isOnApprovedLeave` is asked once per preceding workday per rest date, so with Friday off -- this market's ordinary configuration -- one row measured **34 statements over a month against 16 over a week**, and four rows over a month went from 22 to **107** (166 with a three-day weekend). The shift term really is gone: zero per-date shift queries in all three configurations. So this change **halves a normally-configured month rather than flattening it**, and `aCompanyWithAWeeklyRestDayStillPaysForEveryRestDateInThePeriod` now asserts the 34 so the next reader cannot take 22 for the whole truth. Batching the rest credit means batched variants inside `LegacyPayrollAttendanceFigures` and `LegacyWeeklyRestCredit`, which payroll shares; the owner's call on 2026-09-23 was to merge this and do that as its own change, with its own parity argument. **That change is D-279, which closes this row: ten rows over a month went from 286 statements to 38.** |
| Rollback | Revert the commit. No schema, no migration, no data change, and no change to any number the page prints. What an operator would see if this were wrong: the attendance report showing a different shift for a date than the detail view does for the same employee -- the warm test is what makes that a build failure rather than a support ticket. The lexical comparison the walk uses is correct only while `effective_from` is a `DATE`; that dependency is now stated in the method's javadoc, and `check_legacy_schema_drift.py` is what would catch a widening. |
| Related | **D-099** (the session data source's own per-checkout statement, which is why the budget tests wrap a plain `DriverManagerDataSource`), the `QueryCounter` javadoc's earlier finding of this same shape in `payslips/list.php`'s enrichment loop, and **D-279**, which closes the term this one left. (An earlier revision of this row cited **R-060** for round-trip budget reasoning; R-060 is an uncommitted hr-legacy feature and contains none. Corrected rather than left to be followed.) |

## D-277: The App API Stops Reproducing `workforce_planning`'s Cross-Tenant Disclosure

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Status | **ACCEPTED 2026-09-23 by the repository owner.** Not an agent decision: D-131 records that a tenant-boundary parity question of this kind may not be decided by an agent, and this reverses D-131. The owner was given the live attack path, D-131's own answer, the fact that D-177 had already hardened the same table on the dashboard surface, and three options -- harden the API surface, keep parity and only add the missing test, or harden the stats read alone. The answer was to harden the API surface. |
| Decision | **`apis/api/workforce_planning/` validates the three org keys on every path that writes them, and `apis/api/dashboard/stats.php` scopes the read.** `create.php` already checked `branch_id`, `department_id` and `job_title_id` against the caller's company; `save_target.php` checked none and `update.php` wrote them straight through its four-column whitelist. The three checks are extracted and used by all three paths, answering 404 `branch_not_found` / `department_not_found` / `job_title_not_found` as `create` already did. `update` validates each key **the body actually carries**, so an edit naming none of them is unaffected. Zero remains "no department" rather than a foreign key, as the schema and legacy both treat it. `update` binds **the long it checked**, not PDO's string: `(int) 28011.9` is 28011 and owned, while the bound string `"28011.9"` is rounded to 28012 by MariaDB on an INT column under this datasource's empty `sql_mode`, so a check and its write could name different companies; `create.php`'s insert already bound the coerced long, so the three paths now agree on what one input means. Editing checks **ownership only** -- `create` keeps legacy's `job_title_belongs_to_company()`, which also requires `is_active = 1`, but a target planned against a title deactivated afterwards is still the tenant's own row, and an older client re-sending it must not be refused. On the read side every join that reaches a joined row or an employee through an org id relates it to the row's own company: the dashboard's planning query (join and headcount subquery), the three `LEFT JOIN`s behind `list.php`, `one.php` and `create.php`'s re-read, the five sibling aggregates in `LegacyDashboardStore` that walk from a scoped `departments` or `branches` row out to `employees`, and `HomeStore`'s copy of the planning chart on the admin home page. |
| Why | D-131 chose parity on 2026-08-30 and that answer held for 24 days. What changed is not the code but what is known about it: the disclosure is **live and reachable by any tenant's ordinary `company_admin` or `hr` token in two calls**, the desktop client calls this endpoint, `hr-legacy#33` is still open upstream with no date, and the same table's dashboard port had already been hardened under D-177 -- so the port already held two answers for one table and the inconsistency was load-bearing in the wrong direction. R-046's rule is that a missing authorization check is never imported; D-058's parity default is what argued the other way. The owner resolved it toward R-046 for this surface. |
| Why the read side too | **A write-side check cannot do anything about rows already written.** `save_target` was unvalidated for the whole life of this surface, so production data may already contain rows whose `department_id` points at another company; every one of them would keep disclosing that department's name and its active **headcount** through `dashboard/stats.php`, which is one field more than `list.php` ever leaked. Scoping the query is the only thing that closes those, and the same argument reaches further than the first revision of this row applied it: `list.php`, `one.php` and `create.php`'s re-read joined `branches`, `departments` and `job_titles` on id alone too, so a planted row still named all three. They are `LEFT JOIN`s, so scoping them leaves the row in its owner's list with the name absent rather than dropping it, which the inner join in `stats.php` does. **Not byte-identical for every clean row**, which this row claimed until the review: adding `e.company_id = wt.company_id` to a headcount changes the count exactly when another tenant's employee points at this company's department, and that is the case the predicate exists for -- `employees.department_id` and `employees.branch_id` carry no foreign key either. The change is in the tenant's favour and is now pinned by a test rather than asserted here. |
| Divergences from legacy | **Deliberate, and the first on this module.** Legacy's `save_target.php`, `update.php` and `stats.php` are unchanged and still carry the defect; `hr-legacy#33` stays open for legacy's own sake. The port now answers 404 where legacy answers 200, on a request no legitimate client makes -- no client has a reason to name a branch, department or job title that is not its own. Everything else about the module stays character-for-character legacy's. |
| Regression coverage | **The two regressions D-131 created are inverted, not deleted**, which is the instruction their own javadoc carried: `saveTargetLeaksAnotherCompanysBranchNameThroughTheUntenantedJoin` becomes `saveTargetRefusesAnotherCompanysBranchInsteadOfDisclosingItsName`, asserting 404 and that `list.php` then has no row to read a foreign name through, and `updateAlsoWritesAForeignBranchIdWithoutValidating` becomes `updateRefusesAForeignBranchIdButStillEditsPlannedCountAlone`. That pairing is deliberate: an `update` hardened without it would refuse every edit that changes only `planned_count`, and a refusal-only test would still have passed. New: `LegacyDashboardEndToEndTest.aPlanningRowPointingAtAnotherCompanysDepartmentDisclosesNothing` inserts the planted row **directly**, because the endpoint now refuses to create it -- which is the point, since that is the data shape only the query can protect. After the review round, four more tests: a fractional id is stored as the id that was checked and a fractional foreign id is still refused; an edit may name this company's deactivated job title although `create` still refuses it; a row planted on another company's branch is still listed but names nothing; and another company's employee placed inside this company's department and branch -- with a contract, today's attendance and a penalty -- leaves the **whole `stats.php` response equal to what it was before that row existed**. `HomeStoreWorkforcePlanningTest` covers the admin home chart in both of its modes, including `companyId = 0`, where `scope()` degrades to `1=1` and the predicate has to relate the two tables rather than name one company. **Ten mutants, all dead, with a green control of 29 tests**: `update` binding PDO's string again, editing requiring an active title again, the planning read's branch join on id alone, each of the five sibling aggregates unscoped one at a time, and each of the home chart's two predicates. The pre-round count of four mutants had treated the two stats predicates as one, and the headcount predicate was in fact **untested** -- the scoped join drops the planted row before the subquery runs, so only a clean row with a foreign employee reaches it. Suite: `LegacyWorkforcePlanningEndToEndTest` 13, `LegacyDashboardEndToEndTest` 14, `HomeStoreWorkforcePlanningTest` 2 -- **29 tests, 0 failures**, and 61 over the wider affected set. |
| Also changed | Five documents asserted the leak as current and would have become false claims on merge: `docs/security/threat-model.md`'s risk row (disposition rewritten, severity and history kept, evidence pointers repointed at the inverted tests), `docs/api/existing-endpoint-inventory.md` in both places that describe it, `docs/bootstrap/open-questions.md` (the reversal recorded above the 2026-08-30 resolution, which is kept unedited), D-131's own status line, and `docs/bootstrap/risk-register.md`'s **R-012**, which the first sweep missed: it read "None applied, deliberately" and its Evidence cell still named `saveTargetLeaksAnotherCompanysBranchNameThroughTheUntenantedJoin`, a test this change renamed out of existence. Two class javadocs in the changed files said the same thing and are corrected with them. |
| Review round 1 | A read-only `reviewer` agent on `f7fd2412`, in its own throwaway full clone (`git clone --no-local`, then the head fetched from GitHub), with this worktree read only. **It did not clear the head: one P1, five P2 and two P3.** Codex could not review at all -- its only comment on the pull request is a usage-limit notice. **P1, the blocker: the check and the write converted the same value differently.** `update` validated with `LegacyValues.toPhpLong`, PHP's truncating `(int)` cast, and bound `toPdoBindValue`, which is `toPhpString`; this datasource runs `SET SESSION sql_mode=''`, so MariaDB rounds the bound string on an INT column instead of erroring. `{"branch_id": 28011.9}` therefore checked 28011, which the caller owns, and stored 28012, which another company owns -- and the update's own response returned that company's branch name. Reproduced here before fixing, not taken on report: the failing assertion read `branch_name="Victim HQ"`, `job_title_id=28032`. Branch, department and job-title ids share one global auto-increment, so tenants interleave and `ownId+1` is a real reach for every id a tenant owns. `create` and `save_target` bind the coerced long, so the three paths disagreed about one input; `update` now binds the long it checked. **P2, the fix broke a legitimate client:** reusing `job_title_belongs_to_company()`, which also requires `is_active = 1`, made a full-row PUT that re-sent an own, since-deactivated job title answer 404, and the tenant could not then edit even `planned_count` on that row. Editing is a tenant question, not an activity one, so `update` and `save_target` check ownership alone and `create` keeps legacy's stricter rule. **P2, the read side was half-done:** this entry's own argument -- a write-side check cannot reach rows already written -- applies verbatim to `list.php`, `one.php` and `create.php`'s re-read, which still joined all three name tables on id alone, and whose only coverage had just been inverted away. **P2, a surviving mutant:** removing the headcount predicate left the suite green, because the scoped join drops the planted row before the subquery runs. **P2, one instance fixed and six left:** five sibling aggregates in the same store walk from a scoped `departments` or `branches` row out to `employees` with no company predicate, and `HomeStore` holds a literal copy of the pre-fix planning query that draws another company's department name and headcount on the admin home page. **P2, the document sweep missed `risk-register.md`'s R-012**, the repository's own risk authority, whose Evidence cell still named a test this branch had renamed out of existence. **Two P3 record findings, both fixed rather than deferred:** two class javadocs in the changed files still asserted the leak as current, and this entry's "byte-identical for a clean row" overstated the read-side change. All eight are fixed on this branch; none was deferred to an issue. **What the reviewer confirmed by execution rather than reading:** `create` and `save_target` bind the coerced long and were never vulnerable to the fractional trick; zero, negative, boolean, array, object, overflowing and non-numeric ids are all refused or harmless; a duplicated JSON key is read the same way by the check and the write, so there is no TOCTOU; `summary.php` is the same handler object as `list.php` and not a second write path; no bulk or import route touches this table; and `planned_count` alone, a full-row PUT of own ids, `department_id: 0` and create-then-update all still answer 200. **What it could not verify:** whether production holds mis-pointed rows or planning rows on deactivated job titles, which is the size of this today. |
| Rollback | Revert the commit. No schema, no migration, no data change. What an operator would see if this were wrong: a `company_admin` or `hr` client receiving 404 `branch_not_found` on a planning save that used to succeed, which means it was naming a branch outside its own company -- and the log line to look for is that 404 against `workforce_planning/save_target.php` or `update.php`. A clean client cannot produce it. |
| Related | **D-131** (the parity answer this reverses) and **D-141** (the owner ruling that accepted it), **D-177** (the same table hardened on the dashboard surface, which this brings the API into line with), **D-176** (an edit may not move a row onto another company's key), **R-046** (never import a missing authorization check), **D-058** (the parity default this departs from), `hr-legacy#33`. |
